choose-harness.definition: A harness is the engine behind an agent. It decides when to call the AI model, what to send it, and which tools to run.
choose-harness.analogy: Think of it like a chef and a kitchen: the model supplies the skill, and the harness sets up the tools and directs the work.

blocks.label: AI model
blocks.plain: Supplies the reasoning that every harness uses.

blocks.label: Standard harness
blocks.plain: Follows the topics and rules you write. Best for steady, repeatable chats.

blocks.label: Microsoft Copilot harness
blocks.plain: Takes a goal, plans steps, and adapts, for long, multi-step work.

blocks.label: Customer Conversation harness
blocks.plain: Built for customer voice and chat, with specialist sub-agents and human handoff.

flow.label: Scenario
flow.plain: Start with the business process and how the agent must behave.

flow.label: Weigh
flow.plain: Compare how much control, scale, speed, and cost the work needs.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: Pick a harness when the agent is created; the choice shapes its features.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: The parts you can add, and how usage is billed, follow that harness.

flow.label: Revisit
flow.plain: An upgrade copies a standard agent to the Microsoft Copilot harness (preview), one way only.

example.input: Contoso needs an agent that collects every HR request in the same order and routes it to the right team.
example.output: The standard harness fits: topics keep the questions and the handoff in a set order instead of improvising.

whenToUse: Standard: short, bounded work where explicit control and proven channels matter most.
Microsoft Copilot harness: long, multi-step work with files, tools, and changing information.
Customer Conversation harness: customer voice and chat, with a path to a person.
whenNot: Do not move a working standard agent just because a newer option exists.
A heavier harness can add delay and Copilot Credits to a simple task.
Upgrading does not carry over knowledge sources, Power Fx, or child agents.
choose-harness.needToKnow: The harness affects the billing, features, and capabilities of what you build. You pick it when you create the agent, and an agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness cannot be moved back to the standard harness. Later topics explain each building block and say when a harness lacks it.
choose-harness.demo: Show the comparison of the three harnesses on one slide, then walk through one example scenario for each.
choose-harness.askTheRoom: Think of an agent you might build. Does it need to follow a fixed script, or work out its own steps?
choose-harness.sayOutLoud: At Contoso, an HR intake agent must ask the same questions every time. A different agent that prepares customer meeting briefs has to read many sources and adapt as it goes. Those two jobs fit different harnesses.

quiz.q: What does a harness do?
options: It decides when to call the AI model and which tools to run
quiz.why: The harness is the layer between the AI model and the agent's setup. It decides when to call the model, what to send, and which tools to call.

quiz.q: Which harness follows the topics and rules that you write?
quiz.why: The standard harness is built for rule-based agents and structured, repeatable conversations.

quiz.q: Can an agent built on the Microsoft Copilot harness move back to the standard harness?
options: No, it cannot be moved back
Only if it has no tools
quiz.why: Learn says agents on the Microsoft Copilot harness cannot be transferred to the standard harness.

quiz.q: Which harness is built for customer voice and chat, with escalation to a person?
quiz.why: The Customer Conversation harness uses a primary agent and specialist sub-agents, each with its own escalation path.

create-agent.definition: Creating an agent makes the starting object that holds its name, its instructions, and the knowledge and tools you add later.
create-agent.analogy: Think of it like hiring a new team member: you give them a name and a job description before you hand over tools and files.

blocks.label: Name
blocks.plain: The display name people see for the agent.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Plain-language rules for the agent's job, tone, and limits.

blocks.label: Components
blocks.plain: Knowledge, tools, and other agents you add after the first save.

blocks.label: Starting point
blocks.plain: Start blank, or describe the agent in words and let AI draft the details.

flow.label: Idea
flow.plain: A maker describes the agent in words, or starts from a blank agent.

flow.label: Draft
flow.plain: The AI can suggest a name, description, and instructions, plus sources and tools.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The maker reads the draft and fixes anything that looks wrong.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: The agent is saved and is ready for knowledge, tools, and testing.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: The maker tests the agent and keeps refining it.

example.input: A Contoso maker describes a help agent for new employees in one short paragraph.
example.output: The maker gets a draft name, description, and instructions to review and change, and can accept or ignore suggested sources and tools.

whenToUse: Every project starts here, because everything else hangs off the agent.
Start from a description when you want a quick first draft.
Start from blank when you want full control of every detail.
whenNot: Do not treat the generated draft as final; review the name and instructions.
Generated suggestions cover only some sources and tools; add the rest yourself.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness, natural-language creation is a preview feature.
create-agent.needToKnow: The agent is the object that everything else attaches to, so the first choices matter: the harness, the name, and the instructions. The harness decides which parts you can add next. Treat the first version as a draft, and plan to test and improve it.
create-agent.demo: Show an agent created from a one-paragraph description and the draft it produced, then point out what you would change.
create-agent.askTheRoom: What is one job on your team that you could describe to an agent in a short paragraph?
create-agent.sayOutLoud: Creating an agent is like writing a job post and hiring for it. At Contoso, a short paragraph about helping new employees is enough to get a first draft. You still read it and fix it.

quiz.q: What do you create first when you build an agent?
options: The agent itself, which later parts attach to
quiz.why: Everything else, such as knowledge, tools, and skills, is added to the agent after it exists.

quiz.q: Can AI draft a name, description, and instructions from your own words?
options: Yes, and you should review the draft
quiz.why: Starting from a description gives you generated details. You can accept, change, or ignore them.

quiz.q: Do generated suggestions include every kind of tool and knowledge source?
options: No, some kinds are not suggested
quiz.why: Learn says the suggestions cover only some knowledge sources and tools, so you add the rest yourself.

instructions.definition: Instructions are plain-language directions that tell an agent its job, its tone, and what to avoid.
instructions.analogy: Think of it like a job description and a style guide for a new teammate.

blocks.label: Role
blocks.plain: What the agent is for and who it helps.

blocks.label: Tone
blocks.plain: How it should sound, such as formal, friendly, or brief.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Topics to decline or redirect, and when to hand off.

blocks.label: Resource hints
blocks.plain: Which tools or knowledge to use when the choice is not obvious.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person sends a message to the agent.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The agent reads its instructions along with the conversation so far.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: Instructions help it decide which tools, knowledge, or other agents to use.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: They shape the reply: its tone, its scope, and what it declines.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: Makers test and adjust the instructions step by step.

example.input: A person asks Contoso's coffee-ordering agent for legal advice.
example.output: With an instruction to answer only about coffee orders, the agent tells the person it cannot help with that request.

whenToUse: Set the agent's role, tone, and scope in one clear place.
Guide which tool or knowledge source to use when the choice is unclear.
Say what to decline and when to hand off to a person.
whenNot: Instructions cannot use a tool or source the agent does not have.
On the standard harness, do not try to change how citations work in instructions.
On the Customer Conversation harness, long instructions crowd out room for conversation history.
instructions.needToKnow: The agent can only follow instructions about parts it actually has. It picks tools, knowledge, and other agents by their names and descriptions, and your instructions add hints on top. Keep instructions short, and test after each change.
instructions.demo: Show two versions of the same agent, one with vague instructions and one with a clear role, tone, and limits, answering the same question.
instructions.askTheRoom: What is one thing you would never want your agent to answer, and how would you say that in one sentence?
instructions.sayOutLoud: Instructions are the agent's job description. At Contoso, the coffee agent's instructions say it only handles coffee orders, so it politely declines anything else.

quiz.q: What do instructions tell an agent?
options: Its job, its tone, and its limits
quiz.why: Instructions guide the agent's behavior, tone, and scope.

quiz.q: Can an instruction make the agent use a tool it does not have?
options: No, the tool must be added first
Yes, if the instruction is long enough
quiz.why: An agent cannot act on instructions about tools, knowledge, or agents it does not have. You configure them first.

quiz.q: Besides instructions, what helps the agent pick the right tool?
options: Clear names and descriptions for each tool
quiz.why: The orchestrator uses the names and descriptions of tools, knowledge sources, and agents to decide what to call.

model-orchestration.definition: The model is the AI that reads and writes. Orchestration is how the agent decides which tool, knowledge source, or other agent to use for each request.
model-orchestration.analogy: Think of it like a dispatcher who reads each request and sends it to the right team.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.plain: The AI that reasons and writes; choose it for quality, speed, and cost.

blocks.label: Orchestrator
blocks.plain: Reads each request and picks tools, knowledge, topics, or agents.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Names and descriptions are the main clues the orchestrator uses.

blocks.label: Classic mode
blocks.plain: Standard harness only: picks a topic by matching trigger phrases.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks a question, or an event starts the agent.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The orchestrator reads the request and the recent conversation.

flow.label: Select
flow.plain: It picks the tools, knowledge, topics, or agents that fit.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: It calls what it picked and collects the results.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The model writes one reply from everything that came back.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: A maker can look at what was picked to see why.

example.input: A person asks, 'What is the weather like in Seattle?' and the agent has a weather tool.
example.output: The agent picks the weather tool, fills in the city from the question, and writes the answer.

whenToUse: Let the agent choose among many tools and sources by itself.
Handle requests that need more than one step or more than one source.
Match the model to the job: faster for simple work, deeper for hard reasoning.
whenNot: Do not use preview or experimental models for production agents.
Look-alike descriptions confuse the agent, so make each one distinct.
More reasoning can mean more delay and cost for simple tasks.
model-orchestration.dataNote: Data sent to a preview model might be handled outside your region. Experimental models can do the same.
model-orchestration.needToKnow: The orchestrator chooses with names and descriptions, so clear wording matters more than clever tricks. The model you pick sets reasoning depth, quality, speed, and cost. On the standard harness you can choose generative or classic orchestration; the Microsoft Copilot harness always uses its own enhanced orchestration.
model-orchestration.demo: Show the activity view after a question that needs two things, such as a tool and a knowledge source, and name what the agent picked.
model-orchestration.askTheRoom: When two of your tools sound alike, how would a person tell which one to use? How would an agent?
model-orchestration.sayOutLoud: The orchestrator is like a good receptionist. It reads what you need and sends you to the right desk. At Contoso, that desk might be a weather tool, a store-hours topic, or a policy document.

quiz.q: What is the main clue an orchestrator uses to pick a tool?
quiz.why: Learn calls the descriptions of topics, tools, agents, and knowledge sources the most important factor.

quiz.q: Which kind of model should you avoid for production agents?
quiz.why: Learn says preview and experimental models are for exploring and testing, not for production.

quiz.q: What can generative orchestration do on the standard harness?
options: Pick among topics, tools, knowledge, and agents
quiz.why: With generative orchestration, the agent can pick one or more topics, tools, knowledge sources, or other agents for a request.

quiz.q: Which is true about a deep model compared with a general one?
options: It usually costs more and is slower
It cannot reason in several steps
quiz.why: Learn lists deep models as best for multistep reasoning, with the highest latency and cost.

knowledge.definition: Knowledge is the content an agent reads so it can answer from your information instead of guessing.
knowledge.analogy: Think of it like giving a new employee the company handbook and key files before their first day.

blocks.label: Source
blocks.plain: A place the agent can read, such as a site, files, or business data.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: A name and note that help the agent decide when to use the source.

blocks.label: Search
blocks.plain: The agent looks through sources for passages that match the question.

blocks.label: Citation
blocks.plain: A note that shows which source an answer came from.

blocks.label: Permissions
blocks.plain: Sign-in sources return only what the asking person is allowed to see.

flow.label: Question
flow.plain: A person asks something that might be answered in your content.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The agent decides whether any knowledge source could help.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: It searches the connected sources for passages that match.

flow.label: Check access
flow.plain: For sign-in sources, only content that person may see comes back.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The model writes an answer from what it found.

flow.label: Cite
flow.plain: In chat, the reply can include citations that link to the source.

example.input: {sampleQuestion}
example.output: An answer written from your connected content, with a citation in chat that shows where it came from.

whenToUse: Answer questions from your own policies and files.
Keep answers current when the source content changes.
Limit the agent to answers from approved sources.
whenNot: Knowledge only reads content; it cannot take actions. Use a tool for that.
Answers can still be wrong; tell people to check important ones.
On the Customer Conversation harness, sources that need sign-in work only in chat.
knowledge.dataNote: Sources that need sign-in return only what the signed-in person can see. On the standard harness, uploaded files are stored in Dataverse, and public website searches go through Bing.
knowledge.needToKnow: Knowledge grounds answers in your content, but the agent picks sources by their names and descriptions, so write them well. Sources that need sign-in return only what the asking person may see. Reading content is not the same as acting on it; actions need tools.
knowledge.demo: Ask the same question with and without a knowledge source connected, and show the difference and the citation.
knowledge.askTheRoom: Where does the answer to your team's most common question live today? Who can open it?
knowledge.sayOutLoud: Think of the Contoso employee handbook. Without it, the agent guesses. With it connected, the agent finds the leave policy and shows where the answer came from.

quiz.q: What is knowledge for an agent?
options: Content it reads to answer questions
quiz.why: Knowledge sources ground the agent in your organization's content instead of only its general training.

quiz.q: What does a citation tell the reader?
options: Which source an answer came from
quiz.why: In chat, a response can include citations that link to the knowledge source it used.

quiz.q: A knowledge source that needs sign-in returns content that...
options: The signed-in person is allowed to see
quiz.why: With user authentication, the agent surfaces only content that the specific user can access.

quiz.q: How can the agent tell when to use a source?
options: By the source's name and description
It always searches every source at once
quiz.why: Learn advises updating the name and description of a source so the agent can tell when to use it.

tools.definition: A tool is an action an agent can take, such as looking up a record, creating a ticket, or sending a message.
tools.analogy: Think of it like the apps on a phone: each one lets the agent do one specific thing.

blocks.label: Tool
blocks.plain: One action the agent can call, such as creating a ticket.

blocks.label: Connector
blocks.plain: A ready-made link to another service that supplies many tools.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: What the agent reads to decide when to call the tool.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: The details a tool needs, such as an order number.

blocks.label: Credentials
blocks.plain: Whose sign-in the tool uses: the person chatting, or the maker.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: A person asks for something that needs an action or live data.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The agent reads each tool's name and description and picks one.

flow.label: Gather
flow.plain: It gathers the details the tool needs from the conversation.

flow.label: Sign in
flow.plain: The tool runs with the person's own sign-in or the maker's, as set up.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The tool calls the other system and returns its result.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent uses the result to write its reply.

example.input: A Contoso employee says, 'I am locked out of my account.'
example.output: The agent picks a password reset tool, asks the person to confirm, runs it, and reports the result.

whenToUse: Look up live data from another system instead of guessing.
Create or update records, send notifications, or start a process.
Reach a service that has a ready-made connector or your own connector.
whenNot: Tools take actions; use knowledge when the agent only needs to read documents.
Too many look-alike tools confuse the agent, so keep the set small and clear.
A data policy can block a tool; blocked tools cannot be added.
tools.dataNote: A tool can run with each person's own credentials, so people reach only data they may see, or with the maker's credentials. Data policies decide which tools are allowed.
tools.needToKnow: The agent picks a tool from its name and description, so clear wording matters. Connectors, custom connectors, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, workflows, and computer use are all ways to supply tools. Who the tool signs in as decides what data it can reach.
tools.demo: Show the activity view after a request that needs an action, and point out the tool the agent picked and the details it filled in.
tools.askTheRoom: Which three actions would save your team the most time if an agent could do them?
tools.sayOutLoud: Knowledge lets an agent read. Tools let it act. When a Contoso employee is locked out, the agent can run a password reset tool, but only after it asks them to confirm.

quiz.q: What helps decide whether the agent calls a tool?
options: The tool's name and description, with the chat and instructions
The size of the tool's file
quiz.why: The orchestrator evaluates each message and uses the tool's name and description, plus the conversation and instructions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a kind of tool?
quiz.why: Connectors, MCP servers, and workflows are among the tool types an agent can use.

quiz.q: If a tool runs with end user credentials, what data can it reach?
options: Only data that person may see
quiz.why: With end user credentials, people only get data they are allowed to see.

quiz.q: What can stop a maker from adding a tool?
options: A data policy set by admins
quiz.why: Data policies control which tools makers can add, and a blocked tool cannot be selected.

skills.definition: A skill is a reusable, saved ability that guides an agent through one kind of task when a request matches it.
skills.analogy: Think of it like a recipe card that the agent pulls out only when the request calls for it.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: Tells the agent when the skill applies; clear wording helps it match.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Written steps and rules for the task, often in Markdown.

blocks.label: Skill types
blocks.plain: On the Customer Conversation harness: generative skills or fixed-step topic skills.

blocks.label: Prompt tool
blocks.plain: On the standard harness, a saved prompt the agent can run as a tool.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: A person asks for a task the agent has a skill for.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: The agent compares the request with each skill's description.

flow.label: Activate
flow.plain: The matching skill's instructions guide the agent for this task.

flow.label: Combine
flow.plain: The skill can tell the agent to use a tool in a particular way.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent finishes the task and answers in the format the skill describes.

example.input: A Contoso manager asks the agent to review an expense report against company rules.
example.output: The agent uses its expense-policy skill and follows the saved steps instead of guessing.

whenToUse: Capture know-how once and reuse it across agents.
Give the agent a new ability without changing its core instructions.
Make a multistep task repeatable and easier to review.
whenNot: Skills give instructions, not connections; use a tool to reach another service.
On the Customer Conversation harness, keep skills short and few to save context.
On the standard harness, 'skill' means a different, code-based kind; use prompt tools.
skills.needToKnow: A skill packages instructions, while a tool connects to a service, and the agent picks both by their descriptions. Skills follow a pattern where the agent loads only the context it needs, when it needs it. Check the harness when you read Learn, because the word skill means different things on the standard harness.
skills.demo: Show a skill's name, description, and instructions, then ask a question that matches it and show the agent using it.
skills.askTheRoom: What task does your team do the same way every time, with steps that someone could write down?
skills.sayOutLoud: A skill is a recipe card. Contoso writes down how to check an expense report once. Any agent that has the card follows the same steps.

quiz.q: What does a skill's description do?
options: Helps the agent decide when to use the skill
quiz.why: The orchestration runtime uses the description to decide when to activate a skill.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a skill and a tool?
options: A skill gives instructions; a tool connects to a service
quiz.why: Skills are self-contained instructions. Tools connect to external services.

quiz.q: Which harness has both generative skills and topic skills?
quiz.why: The Customer Conversation harness supports generative skills, which reason in the moment, and topic skills, which follow authored steps.

Create a skill for an agent (Customer Conversation)

mcp.definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that lets a server offer tools to an agent, so the agent can use them.
mcp.analogy: Think of it like a universal plug: one standard connection lets many different tools work with the agent.

blocks.label: MCP server
blocks.plain: A program that publishes tools and resources an agent can use.

blocks.label: Tools
blocks.plain: Actions the server offers, with the names and descriptions it supplies.

blocks.label: Resources
blocks.plain: File-like data the agent can read for more context.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: The sign-in details the server needs; they vary by server.

blocks.label: Policies
blocks.plain: Power Platform data policies still govern access.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: A maker connects a server from a list or by its web address.

flow.label: Learn
flow.plain: The agent reads the names and descriptions of the server's tools.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for something that one of those tools can do.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: The agent picks the tool and calls the server with the needed details.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The server sends back a result, and the agent writes the reply.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: If the server changes its tools, the agent reflects the change.

example.input: A person asks, 'Where is order 1001?' and the agent is connected to a Contoso order server.
example.output: The agent calls the server's order-lookup tool and uses the details it returns to write the answer.

whenToUse: Reach custom services, databases, or internal systems through one standard.
Reuse tools that another team already published on a server.
Let the server owner update tools without changing the agent.
whenNot: Do not connect servers you do not trust; their descriptions can steer the agent.
On the standard harness, MCP needs generative orchestration turned on.
Unclear tool descriptions make answers less reliable; ask the server owner to improve them.
mcp.dataNote: For a non-Microsoft server, you are responsible for the tools and data you reach through it.
mcp.needToKnow: The server owner controls the tools and the words that describe them, and the agent relies on those words. So review what a server exposes, and connect only servers you trust. Each server also counts toward the total number of tools an agent can host.
mcp.demo: Show an agent using a tool from a connected server, and the activity view showing which tool ran and what it returned.
mcp.askTheRoom: Which system in your company could offer its actions to agents through one standard connection?
mcp.sayOutLoud: MCP is like a universal plug. Instead of building a new connection for every tool, a team publishes its tools on a server, and any agent that trusts the server can use them.

quiz.q: What does an MCP server publish?
quiz.why: An MCP server exposes tools and resources, and Copilot Studio supports both.

quiz.q: Why should you review a server before connecting it?
options: Its tool names and descriptions can influence the agent
quiz.why: The agent uses the names, descriptions, inputs, and outputs the server publishes, and these can influence how the agent behaves.

quiz.q: If the server owner changes a tool, what happens in the agent?
options: Nothing, until you rebuild the agent
quiz.why: Copilot Studio dynamically reflects changes that the server makes to its tools and resources.

hooks.definition: A hook runs a workflow automatically at a set moment in an agent's work, such as before a tool runs.
hooks.analogy: Think of it like a door sensor: it reacts every time, and no one has to decide.

blocks.label: Event
blocks.plain: The moment it listens for, such as a session start or tool call.

blocks.label: Workflow
blocks.plain: The action that runs when the event fires; today it is always a workflow.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.plain: Tool events can be limited to chosen tools, or apply to all.

blocks.label: Response
blocks.plain: What the workflow returns can add context or change what happens next.

flow.label: Event
flow.plain: Something happens, such as a session starting or a tool about to run.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The workflow tied to that event runs and receives details about what happened.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The workflow checks rules, logs the event, or prepares extra context.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: It can add context or change values, and can block a call before a tool runs.

flow.label: Continue
flow.plain: The agent carries on; if the hook returns nothing, it uses its normal behavior.

example.input: Before the agent calls a tool that sends an order, a hook checks the request against a Contoso rule.
example.output: If the request breaks the rule, the workflow returns a denial and the tool call is blocked. Otherwise it goes ahead.

whenToUse: Apply a rule every single time, not only when the agent judges it relevant.
Log every tool call, or write an audit record.
Add the same background context at the start of every session.
Check a tool call against policy before it runs.
whenNot: A failed hook does not stop the agent; never rely on one alone.
Only the check before a tool runs can block an action.
Hooks exist only on the Microsoft Copilot harness, and they are in preview.
hooks.dataNote: Each hook receives details about the conversation, the user, and the agent. Prompts, tool results, and errors can hold content the agent did not produce, so check them first.
hooks.needToKnow: Tools run when the agent decides they fit, but hooks run every time their event happens. A hook uses a published workflow, and it applies to users only after you publish the agent. Hooks help with rules, logging, and context, but they are not a complete safeguard on their own.
hooks.demo: Show a workflow tied to the moment before a tool runs, then show the agent being stopped when a rule is broken.
hooks.askTheRoom: What is one rule at your company that must be checked every time, not just when someone remembers?
hooks.sayOutLoud: A tool is like asking a helper to do something when they think it fits. A hook is like a rule that always fires, such as logging every purchase at Contoso.

quiz.q: How is a hook different from a tool?
options: A hook runs every time its event happens
The agent chooses a hook when it seems relevant
quiz.why: A tool runs only when the agent judges it relevant. A hook runs every time its event fires.

quiz.q: Which moment can block an action?
quiz.why: Learn says the event before a tool runs is the only one that can block an action.

quiz.q: What does the agent do if a hook fails?
options: Carries on as if the hook returned nothing
quiz.why: Hooks do not stop the agent when they fail, so do not use one as your only safeguard.

subagents.definition: A subagent or connected agent is another agent that your agent hands part of a job to, so each agent can stay focused.
subagents.analogy: Think of it like a front desk that sends each visitor to the right specialist.

blocks.label: Primary agent
blocks.plain: The front-door agent that reads each request and decides who handles it.

blocks.label: Sub-agent
blocks.plain: A specialist built inside the primary agent (a child agent on the standard harness).

blocks.label: Connected agent
blocks.plain: A separate agent with its own owner, settings, and publishing.

blocks.label: Outside agents
blocks.plain: Agents hosted elsewhere, such as in Microsoft Foundry, can also connect.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Names and descriptions tell the primary agent where to send a request.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks the primary agent for something.

flow.label: Route
flow.plain: The primary agent compares the request with each specialist's description.

flow.label: Hand off
flow.plain: It sends the specialist a task and, if allowed, the conversation so far.

flow.label: Work
flow.plain: The specialist runs with its own instructions, tools, and knowledge.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The specialist's result goes back to the primary agent.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The primary agent presents the answer to the person.

example.input: A Contoso customer asks a front-door agent about a charge on their bill.
example.output: The front-door agent routes the question to a billing specialist agent, which answers from its own tools and knowledge.

whenToUse: Split work when one agent has too many look-alike choices.
Let different teams build, own, and publish their own specialist agents.
Reuse one specialist agent from several primary agents.
Group tools and knowledge for one focused task inside one agent.
whenNot: Multi-agent setups are not always needed; start with one agent.
Extra hops add delay, and there is more to test and manage.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness, a connected agent cannot call another connected agent.
subagents.dataNote: The primary agent can pass the conversation so far to a connected agent; on the standard harness you can limit that. For agents outside Copilot Studio, you are responsible for how data is handled.
subagents.needToKnow: The primary agent routes using each specialist's name and description, so overlapping descriptions cause wrong routing. A sub-agent shares the primary agent's settings, while a connected agent keeps its own and can be reused. The model may reword the request, so do not rely on exact wording passing through.
subagents.demo: Show a front-door agent and a specialist agent, ask a question that belongs to the specialist, and show where the request was routed.
subagents.askTheRoom: If your agent had to become three specialists, which three would you pick, and who would own each one?
subagents.sayOutLoud: A multi-agent setup is like a reception desk. Contoso's front-door agent does not know everything. It reads your request and sends you to billing, support, or sales.

quiz.q: Who decides which specialist handles a request?
options: The primary agent, using names and descriptions
quiz.why: The primary agent's orchestration compares the request with each specialist's name and description.

quiz.q: What is a connected agent?
options: A separate agent with its own settings that can be reused
A copy of the same agent
quiz.why: A connected agent keeps its own configuration and lifecycle, so another team can own it and several agents can reuse it.

quiz.q: Why can overlapping descriptions be a problem?
options: The primary agent may route to the wrong specialist
They slow down the network cable
quiz.why: Look-alike names and descriptions make it harder for the orchestrator to route requests correctly.

quiz.q: Which is a good reason to connect a separate agent?
options: A different team owns and publishes it
quiz.why: Separate ownership, publishing, and settings are reasons to use a connected agent instead of a sub-agent.

sdk.definition: Code paths let developers edit agents as files, embed them in apps, or build agents in code with a software development kit (SDK).
sdk.analogy: Think of it like opening the hood of a car that you usually drive from the dashboard.

blocks.label: Local editing
blocks.plain: A Visual Studio Code extension lets developers clone and edit an agent as files.

blocks.label: Agents SDK
blocks.plain: A developer toolkit for building agents in code across many channels.

blocks.label: App client
blocks.plain: Code that connects your own web or native app to a published agent.

blocks.label: Code-built agent
blocks.plain: An agent written in code that a Copilot Studio agent can hand tasks to.

blocks.label: Source control
blocks.plain: Files work with Git, pull requests, and team reviews.

flow.label: Path
flow.plain: A developer picks a path: edit files, embed the agent, or connect code.

flow.label: Pull
flow.plain: For editing, the agent's definition is downloaded as local files.

flow.label: Change
flow.plain: The developer edits the files with normal tools, Git, and reviews.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: Applying uploads changes to the agent, but it does not publish them.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: An app talks to the published agent, or the agent hands work to code.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The team tests the result before release.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants the help agent inside the company's own mobile app.
example.output: The developer uses the Agents SDK client to connect the app to the published agent, instead of the ready-made chat box.

whenToUse: Your team wants Git, code review, and a local editor for agents.
You need the agent inside your own app, with your own sign-in.
Developers already built an agent in code and want to reuse it.
whenNot: For a simple public chat box, the ready-made embed needs no code.
Applying local changes edits the live agent, so review before you apply.
These paths are for developers; the steps assume developer tools.
sdk.dataNote: For a code-built agent outside Copilot Studio, you are responsible for how data flows and is handled.
sdk.needToKnow: These paths work on the same agents the designer uses, not separate ones. Applying local changes updates the agent but does not publish it. The Agents SDK moves messages between channels and your code; it does not decide what the agent says.
sdk.demo: Show an agent definition as local text files next to the same agent in the designer, and a small app talking to it.
sdk.askTheRoom: Does your team already keep code and reviews in Git? What would it mean to treat agents the same way?
sdk.sayOutLoud: Most people build in the web designer. Developers at Contoso may prefer their code editor and Git, or want the agent inside their own app. These paths are for them.

quiz.q: What does the Microsoft 365 Agents SDK help with?
options: Moving messages between channels and your agent code
Writing the agent's answers for you
quiz.why: The SDK handles receiving and sending messages across channels. It does not decide what the agent says.

quiz.q: Does applying local changes publish the agent?
options: No, it only updates the agent
quiz.why: Learn says applying changes is not the same as publishing, and it does not publish the agent.

quiz.q: Who are these code paths mainly for?
quiz.why: The SDK instructions are intended for developers or IT professionals familiar with developer tools.

memory.definition: Memory lets an agent keep useful details from past chats and use them later, so people do not repeat themselves.
memory.analogy: Think of it like a good receptionist who remembers a returning visitor's name and last request.

blocks.label: Captured details
blocks.plain: Facts such as role, preferences, or open requests that the agent keeps.

blocks.label: Per person
blocks.plain: Each agent keeps separate memories for each person.

blocks.label: Expiry
blocks.plain: Memories expire after a set time, which differs by harness.

blocks.label: Control
blocks.plain: Makers turn memory on or off for the agent.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Memory is not chat history or knowledge, and it is not proof.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: A person talks with the agent and shares details or corrections.

flow.label: Capture
flow.plain: If memory is on, the agent keeps a few useful details.

flow.label: Store
flow.plain: The details are saved apart for that person and that agent.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: Later, the same person comes back in a new conversation.

flow.label: Recall
flow.plain: The agent reads related memories before it replies.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: It treats memories as background, not proof, and checks important facts.

example.input: A Contoso customer returns and asks, 'Any update on my request?'
example.output: With memory on, the agent can recall the earlier request and continue from there instead of starting over.

whenToUse: Returning people should not have to repeat their preferences.
Long-running work builds on earlier conversations.
Pick up open requests when a customer comes back.
whenNot: Memory can be wrong or out of date; never treat it as proof.
Do not use it for policies, permissions, or live status; use knowledge and tools.
The standard harness has no memory; it keeps context in topics and variables.
memory.dataNote: Each agent keeps a separate memory for each person, and one person's memories are not shown to another. Memories are deleted after a set time. Turning memory off stops its use but does not delete what is stored.
memory.needToKnow: Memory is saved background about a person, separate from chat history, knowledge, and tools. The agent chooses what to keep, so it may miss details or keep outdated ones. Treat memory as a helper for context, and verify anything important against real sources.
memory.demo: Share a harmless preference with the agent, start a new conversation, and show the agent using it. Then show where a person can see what was remembered.
memory.askTheRoom: What would a returning customer or coworker be glad that your agent remembered, and what should it never keep?
memory.sayOutLoud: Without memory, every chat starts cold. With memory, Contoso's agent can remember a returning customer's open request. It is a helpful note, not proof, so important facts still get checked.

quiz.q: What is memory for an agent?
options: Useful details kept from earlier conversations
A backup copy of the agent
quiz.why: Memory lets an agent carry what it learns, such as preferences and open requests, into later conversations.

quiz.q: Does turning memory off delete what is already stored?
options: No, it only stops the agent from using it
quiz.why: Learn says turning memory off is not a deletion action. Stored memories expire or are deleted separately.

quiz.q: Which harness does not have memory?
quiz.why: Learn lists memory as not supported on the standard harness and supported on the other two.

quiz.q: Should you treat a memory as proof of who someone is?
options: No, it can be wrong or out of date
quiz.why: Memory is context, not an authoritative record. Verify important facts before acting.

files-code.definition: Some agents can create and edit documents and run Python code in a protected space to analyze data and make charts.
files-code.analogy: Think of it like an assistant who works in a private workshop and hands you the finished file.

blocks.label: Request
blocks.plain: A person asks for something that naturally produces a file.

blocks.label: Sandbox
blocks.plain: A protected area where the agent runs code for the task.

blocks.label: Packages
blocks.plain: Ready-made Python tools for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF files, data, and charts.

blocks.label: File card
blocks.plain: The reply shows the file's name, type, preview, and a download.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Created files can be up to 10 megabytes and are kept 28 days.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for a report, spreadsheet, chart, or deck.

flow.label: Work
flow.plain: The agent writes and runs code in its protected area.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: It uses file and data packages to build or edit the file.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The reply includes a file card with a download.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The person can ask for changes, and the agent updates the file.

example.input: A Contoso analyst asks, 'Summarize this sales workbook and make a chart of revenue by region.'
example.output: The agent reads the workbook, runs code to total the numbers, and returns a chart file the person can download.

whenToUse: Create or edit Word, Excel, PowerPoint, or PDF files from a request.
Analyze tables of data, calculate summaries, and draw charts.
Hand back a finished file, not just text in a chat.
whenNot: A file over 10 megabytes is not returned; ask the agent to split it.
The standard and Customer Conversation harnesses do not focus on file work.
Prompts with code interpreter cannot analyze several files at once.
files-code.dataNote: Created files stay with the conversation for 28 days after its last activity, then they are deleted.
files-code.needToKnow: You do not set up file creation; the agent makes a file when a request needs one. Skills tell the agent how to read each file type, and packages give it the code tools. The file card, size limit, and 28-day retention apply on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
files-code.demo: Ask the agent for a small spreadsheet and a chart, then show the file card and the downloaded file.
files-code.askTheRoom: Which report or spreadsheet does your team rebuild by hand every week?
files-code.sayOutLoud: Instead of pasting numbers into chat, a Contoso analyst asks for a revenue chart. The agent runs code in a protected space and hands back a file, like a coworker sending an attachment.

quiz.q: What does the agent return when it makes a file?
options: A file card with a download
quiz.why: The reply includes a created file card with the file name, type, a preview or icon, and a download action.

quiz.q: How large can a created file be?
quiz.why: A created file can be up to 10 megabytes. A larger file is not returned, so ask the agent to split the output.

quiz.q: Which harness is built for creating and editing files?
quiz.why: The Microsoft Copilot harness creates, edits, and reasons over Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF files. The other two do not focus on files.

conversation-design.definition: Conversation design is how you shape a chat so key moments are predictable, such as greetings, questions, forms, and endings.
conversation-design.analogy: Think of it like a script for the moments that must go the same way, with room for free talk around it.

blocks.label: Topic
blocks.plain: A reusable conversation path for one subject, built from steps.

blocks.label: Variable
blocks.plain: A named value the conversation remembers, such as a name or date.

blocks.label: Entity
blocks.plain: A kind of detail the agent finds, such as a date or city.

blocks.label: Adaptive Card
blocks.plain: A card that shows text, images, and buttons inside the chat.

blocks.label: Power Fx
blocks.plain: Formulas that compute values and test conditions in the flow.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: The conversation begins, and a start event can greet the person.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: The agent finds the topic that fits what the person said.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A question step collects a detail and saves it in a variable.

flow.label: Branch
flow.plain: Conditions and formulas decide which path to follow next.

flow.label: Show
flow.plain: Messages or cards present the result in a clear layout.

flow.label: End
flow.plain: An ending step wraps up, such as a short survey or a handoff.

example.input: A Contoso customer says, 'I want to check store hours.'
example.output: A store-hours topic asks which location, saves the answer in a variable, and replies with that location's hours.

whenToUse: Some moments need an exact script, such as disclosures or intake forms.
Collect the same details in the same order every time.
Control greetings, endings, and errors so key moments are predictable.
whenNot: Do not script every question; let the AI handle open-ended ones.
The Microsoft Copilot harness has no topic flows; instructions and hooks do that job.
Cards render differently by channel, so test where people will chat.
conversation-design.needToKnow: Topics give you exact control, and the AI model gives you flexibility. Many agents mix both, and with generative orchestration a topic's description helps the agent choose it. Variables and entities turn free text into values that later steps and tools can use.
conversation-design.demo: Show a short topic with one question, one condition, and one card, then run it and show the saved variable values.
conversation-design.askTheRoom: Which moments in your conversations must never change, and which can be left to the AI?
conversation-design.sayOutLoud: A good chat is part script and part conversation. Contoso's agent greets people the same way every time and always asks for the store location, but it answers open questions freely.

quiz.q: What is a topic?
options: A reusable conversation path for one subject
quiz.why: A topic defines how part of a conversation progresses, and it is built from steps called nodes.

quiz.q: What does a variable do?
options: Remembers a value during the conversation
quiz.why: Variables store a person's responses so you can use them later in the conversation.

quiz.q: Which harness describes behavior in instructions instead of topic flows?
quiz.why: The Microsoft Copilot harness relies on instructions and hooks instead of authored topic flows.

quiz.q: What does an Adaptive Card show in a chat?
quiz.why: An Adaptive Card can hold text, graphics, buttons, and input fields.

workflows.definition: A workflow is a set of automated steps that runs in a set order, started by an agent or by an event.
workflows.analogy: Think of it like an assembly line: each step runs in a set order, whoever starts it.

blocks.label: Trigger
blocks.plain: What starts the workflow: an agent, a schedule, or an event.

blocks.label: Actions
blocks.plain: The steps it runs, such as connectors, branches, and loops.

blocks.label: AI action
blocks.plain: An optional step where a model writes text or reads a document.

blocks.label: Agent link
blocks.plain: Start and reply steps let an agent run it as a tool.

blocks.label: Capacity
blocks.plain: Each action it runs uses Copilot Studio capacity.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks the agent for something repeatable, like an approval.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The agent reads the workflow's description and decides to run it.

flow.label: Send
flow.plain: It passes along the inputs the workflow expects.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The workflow runs its steps in order, calling services as needed.

flow.label: Respond
flow.plain: It sends its results back to the agent.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent tells the person what happened.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks the agent to request time off.
example.output: The agent starts a time-off workflow, which runs the same approval steps every time and returns the result.

whenToUse: Steps must run the same way every time, such as approvals.
Write a row, send a notification, or create a ticket reliably.
Let the agent chat while the workflow does the exact work.
whenNot: Do not use a workflow for open-ended thinking; leave that to the agent.
Long runs may need asynchronous responses, which some channels do not support.
A workflow must be saved and published before an agent can use it.
workflows.dataNote: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, each connector action in a workflow started by an agent uses the calling person's own connections and permissions.
workflows.needToKnow: A workflow follows a defined order of steps, so results are predictable, though AI steps can vary. The agent decides when to run it from its name and description. Each action it runs uses Copilot Studio capacity.
workflows.demo: Show a small workflow with a start step, one action, and a reply step, then ask the agent for something that runs it.
workflows.askTheRoom: Which process on your team must always follow the same steps in the same order?
workflows.sayOutLoud: The agent is the person at the counter, and the workflow is the back-office process. At Contoso, the agent hears the request, and the workflow runs the approval steps the same way every time.

quiz.q: What makes a workflow different from the agent's own reasoning?
options: It follows a defined order of steps
quiz.why: Workflows follow a defined sequence of actions and rule-based branches, which makes the process predictable.

quiz.q: Which two steps let an agent use a workflow as a tool?
options: A step that starts when the agent calls it, and a step that replies to the agent
A step that prints and a step that scans
quiz.why: A workflow used as a tool needs an agent-call start step and a reply step that sends results back.

quiz.q: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, what must happen before an agent can use a workflow?
options: It must be saved and published
quiz.why: Learn says the workflow must be saved and published before the agent can use it.

triggers.definition: A trigger starts an agent from an event, such as an email arriving or a schedule, instead of waiting for a person to chat.
triggers.analogy: Think of it like a doorbell: something happens, and the agent wakes up to respond.

blocks.label: Event
blocks.plain: Something that happens in a connected service, like a new email or file.

blocks.label: Trigger
blocks.plain: Watches for the event and sends its details to the agent.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Tell the agent what to do with each event.

blocks.label: Tools
blocks.plain: The actions the agent can use to respond to the event.

blocks.label: Credentials
blocks.plain: Whose sign-in the agent uses when it runs on its own.

flow.label: Watch
flow.plain: The trigger waits for a chosen event, such as a new email.

flow.label: Fire
flow.plain: When it happens, the trigger sends the event details to the agent.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: The agent reads the details together with its instructions.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: It uses its tools to respond, such as creating a task.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: A maker can look back at what the agent did for each run.

example.input: A new customer account row is added to a Contoso data table.
example.output: The trigger sends the row details to the agent, which checks for a duplicate and creates a follow-up task if it finds one.

whenToUse: React to email, files, or records without someone starting a chat.
Run work on a schedule, such as every morning.
Handle each new item the same way, automatically.
whenNot: On the standard harness, triggers use the maker's sign-in, so review data exposure.
Very frequent triggers use more credits and can reach service limits.
An autonomous agent does not run until you publish it.
triggers.dataNote: Trigger details can hold sensitive information, which the agent might pass along through its tools. Limit what starts a trigger, and tell the agent how to handle the details.
triggers.needToKnow: A trigger only starts the agent. Its instructions and tools decide what happens next, so set up both before you add a trigger. Autonomous agents are billed by usage and run only after you publish them.
triggers.demo: Show a trigger test where a sample event reaches the agent, and the record of what the agent did.
triggers.askTheRoom: What happens on your team every day that an agent could handle without being asked?
triggers.sayOutLoud: Most agents wait for you to speak. An autonomous agent listens for events. At Contoso, a new email can wake an agent that reads it and creates a follow-up task.

quiz.q: What starts an agent that has a trigger?
options: An event in a connected service
quiz.why: Event triggers let an agent act on something that happens, such as an email or a new file, without a person starting a chat.

quiz.q: What decides what the agent does with the event details?
quiz.why: The trigger sends event details to the agent. The agent's instructions and tools decide what it does with them.

quiz.q: When does an autonomous agent start running on its own?
options: As soon as it is drafted
quiz.why: Learn says the agent does not run autonomously until you publish it.

Event trigger overview

integrations.definition: An integration lets an agent use the systems and Microsoft 365 data where your work already lives.
integrations.analogy: Think of it like giving a new colleague logins to the systems they need, with the same access rules as anyone else.

blocks.label: Connector
blocks.plain: A ready-made link to systems such as ServiceNow or Salesforce.

blocks.label: Custom connector
blocks.plain: Your own link, for a service that has no ready-made connector.

blocks.label: Private access
blocks.plain: A data gateway or a virtual network reaches systems that are not public.

blocks.label: Work IQ
blocks.plain: Work IQ (Microsoft Copilot harness) grounds the agent in Microsoft 365 work context.

blocks.label: Contact center
blocks.plain: Customer Conversation harness only: a link that hands chats and calls to a person.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks about a record or task held in a business system.

flow.label: Reach
flow.plain: The agent calls a connector or tool for that system.

flow.label: Sign in
flow.plain: The call uses the person's own access, or the maker's, as configured.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The system sends back records or confirms the action.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent replies, or hands off to a person if it cannot resolve the issue.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks, 'What is the status of my ticket?'
example.output: The agent calls the ticketing system's connector, reads that ticket, and summarizes its status in the chat.

whenToUse: Answers or actions depend on a system of record.
Use Microsoft 365 context such as mail, calendar, and files.
Reach data on a private network through a gateway or virtual network.
whenNot: A data policy can block a connector, so check what your organization allows.
Real-time connector knowledge is a preview feature.
Prefer Work IQ over older workload tools on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
integrations.dataNote: Real-time connector knowledge (preview) indexes only names such as tables and columns, and moves no data. Each request runs in the source system with the person's own access.
integrations.needToKnow: Every integration is a connection plus permissions, so ask first who the agent signs in as. Connectors and tools reach many systems, and a data gateway or virtual network helps when a system is private. Check your organization's data policies before you plan a build.
integrations.demo: Show the agent answering from a connected system, and the sign-in step.
integrations.askTheRoom: Which system holds the answers your people look up most, and who controls access to it?
integrations.sayOutLoud: Most useful answers live in systems the agent does not own. At Contoso, a ticket status lives in the ticketing system. A connector lets the agent look it up, with the same access rules as the person asking.

quiz.q: What does a connector do?
options: Links the agent to another service
quiz.why: Connectors act as wrappers around other services so an agent can read from them and act on them.

quiz.q: Which helps an agent reach data on a private network?
quiz.why: The gateway is a bridge between local data sources and cloud services, and it needs no inbound ports.

quiz.q: What does real-time connector knowledge add to Microsoft's index?
options: Only names such as tables and columns
quiz.why: Learn says Microsoft indexes only metadata, with no data movement. Requests run in the source system at question time.

quiz.q: What can block a connector from being added?
quiz.why: Admins can use data policies to limit which tools and connectors are available.

create-agent.definition: On the standard harness, you create an agent by describing it in your own words, or by starting from a blank agent.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: A short plain-language note about what the agent should do.

blocks.label: Draft
blocks.plain: AI writes a name, description, and instructions from your words.

blocks.label: Suggestions
blocks.plain: It also suggests triggers, channels, knowledge, and tools you can accept or dismiss.

blocks.label: Environment
blocks.plain: The agent lives in an environment, and you need permission there.

blocks.label: Blank start
blocks.plain: A blank agent gives full control when you want no draft.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: The maker describes the agent in a short paragraph.

flow.label: Generate
flow.plain: The AI writes a starting name, description, and instructions.

flow.label: Suggest
flow.plain: It offers suggested sources and tools, which are not kept after the session.

flow.label: Set up
flow.plain: Copilot Studio sets up the agent, which uses Microsoft Entra ID sign-in by default.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The maker reviews, tests, and improves the agent.

example.input: A Contoso maker writes a short description of an agent that answers questions about store hours.
example.output: Copilot Studio drafts a name, description, and instructions, and suggests sources and tools that the maker can add or dismiss.

whenToUse: You want a fast first draft to react to.
You are still shaping the idea and want suggestions.
Start blank if natural-language creation is not available to you.
whenNot: Describing an agent in words is not available in a sovereign cloud.
You cannot change an agent's primary language after you create it.
Suggestions are temporary and cover only some sources and tools.
create-agent.dataNote: When you give feedback on a suggestion, you are asked whether to share context data with Microsoft.

learn.title: Create and delete agents
FAQ for the agent creation from natural language experience

mc-create-agent.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, you create an agent by naming it and writing its instructions, then adding knowledge, tools, and skills.

blocks.label: Name
blocks.plain: The display name people see for the agent.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Plain-language rules for the agent's role, tone, and limits.

blocks.label: First save
blocks.plain: The last name before the first save sets a fixed system name.

blocks.label: Components
blocks.plain: Knowledge, tools, skills, connected agents, a model, and memory come next.

blocks.label: Workspace
blocks.plain: One workspace covers building, testing, evaluating, and monitoring.

flow.label: Name
flow.plain: The maker names the agent, and can set its language and solution first.

flow.label: Instruct
flow.plain: The maker writes the role, tone, and rules in plain language.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: On the first save, the system name is fixed.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: Knowledge, tools, skills, connected agents, a model, and memory come next.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker previews, evaluates, and shares the agent, then publishes it.

flow.label: Watch
flow.plain: Building, testing, and evaluating can use Copilot Credits.

example.input: A Contoso maker names a new benefits agent and describes its role and tone.
example.output: The agent is saved with those instructions, and the maker can add knowledge, tools, and skills to it.

whenToUse: The work is long and multi-step, and may involve files or tools.
You want to steer the agent mainly with plain-language instructions.
You want knowledge, tools, skills, and memory in one workspace.
whenNot: An agent here cannot be moved back to the standard harness.
Dataverse for Teams environments do not support this harness.
Natural-language creation on this harness is a preview feature.

learn.title: Create a new agent (Microsoft Copilot)
About agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness

agent-instructions.definition: On the standard harness, instructions help the agent pick tools, knowledge, topics, or other agents, fill tool inputs, and write replies.

blocks.label: Role and scope
blocks.plain: What the agent covers and what it leaves alone.

blocks.label: Resource hints
blocks.plain: Instructions can name tools, topics, agents, and variables the agent should use.

blocks.label: Guardrails
blocks.plain: Say what to decline, and how answers should be formatted.

blocks.label: Fixed behavior
blocks.plain: Fallback text, citations, and search retrieval are not changed by instructions.

flow.label: Message
flow.plain: A person writes to the agent, or a trigger fires.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The agent uses its instructions plus tool and source descriptions to pick what to call.

flow.label: Fill
flow.plain: It fills tool inputs from the conversation and the instructions.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: It writes a reply that follows the guardrails and format you set.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The maker tests small changes one at a time.

example.input: A person asks Contoso's coffee agent about something that has nothing to do with coffee orders.
example.output: An instruction to respond only about Contoso and coffee orders makes the agent say that it cannot help.

whenToUse: Guide which tool or knowledge to use when several could fit.
Set guardrails, such as what to decline.
Shape how answers are formatted, such as a table for order status.
whenNot: For an exact scripted reply, write a topic instead of an instruction.
Multilingual requests in instructions might work but are not guaranteed.
Do not try to override the citation format or the default fallback message.

learn.title: Write agent instructions
Configure high-quality instructions for generative orchestration

mc-instructions.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, instructions are the main way to control behavior, in place of authored topic flows.

blocks.label: Details
blocks.plain: The agent's name and icon, set beside its instructions.

blocks.label: Role and tone
blocks.plain: Purpose, style, and how formal or brief the agent should be.

blocks.label: Boundaries
blocks.plain: What to decline or redirect, and how to handle unclear input.

blocks.label: Handoffs
blocks.plain: When to escalate or hand off, and when to delegate to task agents.

flow.label: Message
flow.plain: A person sends a message.

flow.label: Interpret
flow.plain: The orchestration runtime interprets the instructions each time it responds.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: It decides what to do, how to respond, and what to avoid.

flow.label: Delegate
flow.plain: Instructions can also guide when to hand work to task agents.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The reply follows the agent's tone, scope, and boundaries.

flow.label: Iterate
flow.plain: Makers refine the instructions as they test.

example.input: A person asks a Contoso agent for something outside its job.
example.output: Instructions that name what to decline or redirect tell the agent how to respond.

whenToUse: Set role, tone, and scope in plain language.
Say what to decline or redirect.
Define when to escalate or hand off.
whenNot: Some standard-harness tips fit only topic-based agents; check them first.
On this harness, instructions also control the response language.

learn.title: Configure agent details and instructions (Microsoft Copilot)
About agents powered by the Microsoft Copilot harness

generative-orchestration.definition: On the standard harness, generative orchestration lets the AI pick topics, tools, knowledge, and other agents from their descriptions.

blocks.label: Orchestrator
blocks.plain: Reads each request and picks what to use.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Descriptions of topics, tools, agents, and sources are the main clue.

blocks.label: Classic mode
blocks.plain: The alternative: pick one topic by matching trigger phrases.

blocks.label: Activity map
blocks.plain: A view in the test chat that shows what the agent picked.

flow.label: Message
flow.plain: A person writes a message, or an event starts the agent.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The agent reads the message and the recent conversation.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: It picks one or more topics, tools, knowledge sources, or agents.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: It generates questions for any missing details.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: It runs the chosen parts in sequence.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: It writes one reply from what they returned.

example.input: A person says, 'I need store hours and my nearest store.'
example.output: The agent picks a store-hours topic and a store-locator topic, runs both in turn, and answers both parts.

whenToUse: Questions that have more than one part.
Many topics, tools, and sources to choose from.
Autonomous work that starts from events.
whenNot: Custom entities do not yet work as tool or topic inputs.
More planning rounds can slow replies; test response time.
Similar descriptions make the pick unpredictable.

learn.title: Orchestrate agent behavior with generative AI

knowledge-sharepoint.definition: SharePoint knowledge lets the agent answer from the sites, folders, or lists you register, showing only what each person may read.

blocks.label: Registered place
blocks.plain: The site, folder, or list you point the agent to.

blocks.label: Search scope
blocks.plain: The registered address and its subfolders, never parents or siblings.

blocks.label: Permissions
blocks.plain: People need at least read access, or the agent gives no response.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: A detailed name and description help the agent decide when to use it.

blocks.label: Lists
blocks.plain: Lists work too; up to 10 per agent gives the best results.

flow.label: Question
flow.plain: A person asks something that might be on a registered site.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The agent uses the source's description to judge whether it fits.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: It searches the registered address and everything under it.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: Only content the signed-in person can open is used.

flow.label: Summarize
flow.plain: Generative answers turn the findings into a short, targeted reply.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks about the travel policy kept on a team site.
example.output: The agent searches only the registered site, finds passages the employee can open, and writes a summary.

whenToUse: Your policies and procedures already live in SharePoint.
You want answers that respect each person's access.
You keep table-like data in SharePoint lists.
whenNot: Links inside a document are not followed; add each target as its own source.
Renaming a site or folder can break the source link.
knowledge-sharepoint.dataNote: Answers use only content the signed-in person can open. Selected lists are brought into Dataverse and indexed.

learn.title: Add SharePoint as a knowledge source
Knowledge sources summary

knowledge-files-web.definition: Uploaded files give the agent your own documents, and public websites give it public pages, both as knowledge sources.

blocks.label: Uploaded file
blocks.plain: A document stored securely in Dataverse for the agent to read.

blocks.label: Public website
blocks.plain: A public address that the agent searches through Bing.

blocks.label: Site rules
blocks.plain: The address must be public, indexed by Bing, and at most two levels deep.

blocks.label: File limits
blocks.plain: Up to 500 files, each at most 512 megabytes, and not encrypted.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: A detailed name and description help the agent choose between sources.

flow.label: Question
flow.plain: A person asks something that a file or public page might answer.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: The agent uses the descriptions to decide which source fits.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: It searches the uploaded documents, or sends a Bing search limited to your website.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent writes a conversational answer from what it found.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks a question that only an uploaded handbook answers.
example.output: The agent finds the passage in the uploaded document and answers in a conversational style.

whenToUse: A one-off document is not ready to go into SharePoint.
Authoritative public pages should back an answer.
Public information should extend what the agent knows.
whenNot: Sites that need sign-in, such as wikis and SharePoint, cannot be public websites.
Image, video, audio, and program files cannot be uploaded.
Forum and social pages can produce poor answers.
knowledge-files-web.dataNote: Uploaded files are stored securely in Dataverse. For a website source, the agent sends a search request to Bing.

learn.title: Upload files as a knowledge source
Add a public website as a knowledge source

mc-knowledge.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, you add knowledge one source at a time; there is no general knowledge on or off setting.

blocks.label: Sources
blocks.plain: Websites, SharePoint, OneDrive for Business, uploaded files, and more business systems.

blocks.label: Policy blocks
blocks.plain: An organization's policy can block a source; it then shows as disabled.

blocks.label: Suggestions
blocks.plain: Suggested sources come from other agents in the environment; review each one.

blocks.label: Foundry IQ
blocks.plain: Foundry IQ (a managed knowledge layer) can be connected as a tool.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Update each source's name and description so the agent knows when to use it.

flow.label: Question
flow.plain: A person asks something the agent might answer from knowledge.

flow.label: Evaluate
flow.plain: The orchestration runtime decides whether knowledge sources are needed.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: It searches the relevant sources and retrieves content.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent uses what it found to write a response.

flow.label: Cite
flow.plain: In chat, citations can link to the source; they are not shown in voice.

example.input: {sampleQuestion}
example.output: The agent searches the sources you added, writes an answer, and can show a citation in chat.

whenToUse: Scope the agent to answer only from approved sources.
Ground answers in documents, websites, and business data.
Reuse a knowledge base that another team already tuned in Foundry.
whenNot: Azure AI Search is not a source here; use Foundry IQ instead.
A blocked source cannot be selected; ask your administrator.
Citations are not shown in voice conversations.

learn.title: Add knowledge sources to an agent (Microsoft Copilot)
Knowledge overview for agents (Microsoft Copilot)
Connect to Foundry IQ from an agent (Microsoft Copilot)

connector-tools.definition: A connector tool is one action from a Power Platform connector that the agent can call, such as creating a record or sending a message.

blocks.label: Connector
blocks.plain: A ready-made link to another service, with many possible actions.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: The sign-in used to reach the service; by default it is the person's.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: The wording the agent reads to decide when to call the tool.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Filled by AI from the chat, or set to a fixed value or formula.

blocks.label: Next step
blocks.plain: After it runs: the agent replies, sends a set message, or shows a card.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: A person asks for something that a connector action can do.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The agent reads each tool's name and description and picks one.

flow.label: Fill
flow.plain: It fills in each input from the chat, or uses the value the maker set.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The tool calls the service with the person's connection, or the maker's.

flow.label: Finish
flow.plain: The result returns to the agent, which writes the reply or sends the set response.

example.input: A Contoso employee reports that a laptop cannot reach the company network.
example.output: The agent picks a ticketing connector tool, fills in the details from the chat, and creates a ticket.

whenToUse: Read from or update a service that has a ready-made connector.
Let AI collect the details the action needs.
Call the action from a topic when it must run at an exact moment.
whenNot: Premium connectors are available only in select Copilot Studio plans.
Image generation is not built in; use an outside service through a connector.
A data policy can block a connector.
connector-tools.dataNote: By default, a connector tool uses each person's own credentials, so people reach only data they may see. A maker can choose maker-provided credentials instead.

learn.title: Use Power Platform connectors as tools in Copilot Studio agents
Add tools to custom agents

mc-tools.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, you add connector, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, and workflow tools; the agent picks them by description.

blocks.label: Tool types
blocks.plain: Connectors, MCP servers, and workflows.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Clear, specific names and descriptions tell the agent when to call a tool.

blocks.label: Policy
blocks.plain: A data policy can block a tool, and the reason is shown.

blocks.label: Actions
blocks.plain: For some connectors, you can pick which actions the agent may use.

blocks.label: Files
blocks.plain: Files a tool produces are limited to 10 megabytes each.

flow.label: Message
flow.plain: A person sends a message.

flow.label: Evaluate
flow.plain: The orchestrator decides whether a tool is needed.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: It uses the tool's name, description, and your instructions to choose one.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The tool runs, signing in as the person if it is set up that way.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent uses the result in its reply, with no topic flow to author.

example.input: A Contoso manager asks the agent to create a support ticket.
example.output: The agent picks the 'Create support ticket' tool because its name and description match, and runs it.

whenToUse: Look up live data or take actions in other systems.
Run a repeatable workflow on demand.
Use hundreds of ready-made connector actions.
whenNot: Prompt tools are not supported here; skills replace them.
Computer use is planned, not available yet.
Files over 10 megabytes are not returned.
mc-tools.dataNote: Some tools sign in with each person's own account; people set up that connection the first time the agent needs it.

learn.title: Add a tool to an agent (Microsoft Copilot)
Available tools for agents (Microsoft Copilot)
Tools overview for agents

mc-memory.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, memory keeps short notes about a person, like their role and preferences, for later chats.

blocks.label: What it keeps
blocks.plain: Role, preferences, feedback, ongoing work, and where to find things.

blocks.label: Who sees it
blocks.plain: Memories are private to each person; makers and others cannot see them.

blocks.label: How long
blocks.plain: Memories are deleted after 28 days of inactivity.

blocks.label: Managing
blocks.plain: People can view and delete their memories in a portal or in chat.

blocks.label: Control
blocks.plain: Turning memory off stops saving and use, but does not delete.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: A person shares a role, a preference, or a correction.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: The agent decides what is worth keeping, guided by its rules and instructions.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: Short plain-text notes are saved for that person's account.

flow.label: Later
flow.plain: In a new conversation, the agent reads related memories first.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: It treats them as background, and follows the current conversation if they differ.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: It checks that a remembered file or setting still exists before acting.

example.input: A Contoso buyer who prefers tables returns and asks for a new supplier comparison.
example.output: The agent remembers the preference and can show the comparison as a table.

whenToUse: People return and should not repeat their role or preferences.
Long-running work builds on earlier corrections.
Automated runs under the same account keep useful context.
whenNot: Memory can be wrong or out of date; check important facts.
It is not a source of authority, and it cannot grant permissions.
In some regions, memory may still be in preview.
