mc-memory.dataNote: Memories sit in Microsoft-managed storage, kept apart for each tenant, agent, and user. They are deleted after 28 days of no use.

learn.title: Memory (Microsoft Copilot)
Memory management and privacy

cc-memory.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, memory carries a customer's recent context for 30 days, so the next chat can pick up.

blocks.label: Built-in context
blocks.plain: Customer name, open requests, and a summary of past conversations.

blocks.label: Custom fields
blocks.plain: Up to five fields you define, such as a membership tier.

blocks.label: Update modes
blocks.plain: Keep only the newest value, or keep a dated list of every value.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Instructions can use memory values to greet and resume open requests.

blocks.label: Channels
blocks.plain: A shared contact identifier links chat and voice memories.

flow.label: Talk
flow.plain: A customer talks with the agent, or with a person in the contact center.

flow.label: Extract
flow.plain: If memory is on, key details are extracted and summarized.

flow.label: Keep
flow.plain: The details are kept for a 30-day window.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The customer comes back by chat or phone.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: The agent reads the context and can welcome them back and resume an open request.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: It treats the context as possibly incomplete, and checks facts before big actions.

example.input: A returning Contoso customer calls about an unfinished order change.
example.output: The agent welcomes them back, mentions the open request, and asks which item to handle first.

whenToUse: Resume an unresolved request when a customer returns.
Personalize a greeting with the remembered name.
Carry context between chat and voice when customers are identified.
whenNot: Do not use it as proof of identity, authorization, or account state.
It is short-term context, not a long-term customer profile.
Without a shared identifier, chat and voice memories stay separate.
cc-memory.dataNote: Each agent keeps a separate memory for each customer, for 30 days. Turning memory off does not delete what is stored.

learn.title: Memory (Customer Conversation)
FAQ for Memory (Customer Conversation)

work-iq.definition: Work IQ (a Microsoft 365 context layer) gives agents live work details, like mail and calendar, within your permissions.

blocks.label: Workloads
blocks.plain: Parts of Microsoft 365 the agent can use, such as mail, calendar, and Teams.

blocks.label: Default
blocks.plain: It is added to every new Microsoft Copilot harness agent, all workloads on.

blocks.label: Layers
blocks.plain: Three layers, called Data, Memory, and Inference, supply the context.

blocks.label: Permissions
blocks.plain: A workload choice never overrides your permissions or policies.

blocks.label: Billing
blocks.plain: It uses Copilot Credits, billed by usage.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks something that depends on their work, like a meeting.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: The agent uses only the workloads the maker left selected.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: Work IQ connects with the person's sign-in and permissions.

flow.label: Fetch
flow.plain: It brings back context from mail, calendar, files, or chats.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent answers from that real-time work context.

example.input: A Contoso sales rep asks the agent to summarize unread emails from today.
example.output: The agent uses the mail workload to read what the rep can access and writes a summary.

whenToUse: Answers depend on a person's mail, calendar, files, or chats.
You want Microsoft 365 context without building each connection.
You want to narrow the agent to only the workloads it needs.
whenNot: Write actions are on by default, within your permissions; scope workloads on purpose.
Some workloads, such as business apps, are still in preview.
Older workload tools like Mail and Teams are a legacy path; prefer Work IQ.
work-iq.dataNote: Work IQ follows your permissions and policies, and admins govern it.

learn.title: Work IQ in Copilot Studio (Microsoft Copilot)

cc-contact-center.definition: Linking an agent to Dynamics 365 Contact Center lets it hand chats to a person, while web chat and Teams Phone keep working.

blocks.label: Maker work
blocks.plain: A maker builds and publishes the agent, then connects its channels.

blocks.label: Web chat
blocks.plain: A chat workstream is created automatically.

blocks.label: Teams Phone
blocks.plain: Connecting only marks voice as connected; an admin finishes the setup.

blocks.label: Admin work
blocks.plain: An admin creates the voice workstream and links and syncs the phone number.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: The maker builds, publishes, and tests the agent.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker connects web chat and Teams Phone to the contact center.

flow.label: Hand over
flow.plain: The maker tells the contact center admin which agent to finish.

flow.label: Finish
flow.plain: The admin completes the voice workstream, linking, sync, and phone number.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: Both channels are tested from start to finish.

flow.label: Go live
flow.plain: If the agent cannot resolve an issue, a person can take over.

example.input: A Contoso customer chats with the agent on the website, and the agent cannot resolve the issue.
example.output: The conversation can be handed to a person in the contact center, through the connected web chat channel.

whenToUse: Customers need a person when the agent cannot resolve an issue.
You already run web chat and Teams Phone and want a handoff.
A maker and a contact center admin share the work.
whenNot: Confirm that Teams Phone works on its own before you connect it.
Connecting channels in the builder is only part of the setup.
Some channels need an environment with Dynamics 365 apps enabled.

learn.title: Deploy an agent (Customer Conversation)

onprem-data-gateway.definition: An on-premises data gateway lets cloud services reach data on your network with no inbound ports.

blocks.label: Gateway
blocks.plain: A Windows program installed on a computer that can reach your data.

blocks.label: Outbound only
blocks.plain: It starts outbound connections to the cloud; no inbound ports are needed.

blocks.label: Two kinds
blocks.plain: The standard gateway serves many users; personal mode is for one person.

blocks.label: Connectors
blocks.plain: Connectors for local business systems use the gateway.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks about data that lives on a private network.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: The agent, or a flow it runs, calls a connector for that system.

flow.label: Bridge
flow.plain: The request reaches the gateway over its outbound connection.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The gateway reads the local data and sends the result back.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent uses the result in its reply.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks about a record kept in a database inside the company network.
example.output: The request reaches the database through the gateway, so the data stays on the network and is not opened to the internet.

whenToUse: Data must stay on your own network.
Many people and systems need one shared bridge.
Business systems sit behind firewalls.
whenNot: Personal mode works with Power BI (a reporting tool) only, not with agents.
Changed credentials can take hours to work, because the gateway caches them.
Size limits apply to gateway requests and responses.
onprem-data-gateway.dataNote: The gateway keeps data on your network and only makes outbound connections to Microsoft cloud services.

learn.title: What is an on-premises data gateway?
On-premises data gateway with access to BAPIs, RFCs, and OData services

vnet-private-connectivity.definition: Virtual network support lets Power Platform reach private resources without the public internet.

blocks.label: Virtual network
blocks.plain: A private Azure network that you control.

blocks.label: Delegated subnet
blocks.plain: Power Platform uses a subnet you delegate for outbound calls.

blocks.label: Supported calls
blocks.plain: Connectors with native support, web requests, and private telemetry can use it.

blocks.label: Environment
blocks.plain: The environment must be a managed environment with virtual network support on.

blocks.label: Network policy
blocks.plain: Your network team applies policies to the outbound traffic.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks about data in a protected resource.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: The agent calls a supported connector or makes a web request.

flow.label: Route
flow.plain: Power Platform sends the call through your delegated subnet.

flow.label: Private path
flow.plain: Traffic travels over your private network, not the public internet.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The resource replies, and the agent answers.

example.input: A Contoso agent needs a record from a database that is closed to the public internet.
example.output: The call goes through the private network, so the database does not need to be available over the internet.

whenToUse: Resources must not be open to the public internet.
You use connectors that support virtual networks.
You want Azure services reached over private endpoints.
whenNot: It needs a managed environment and setup by an administrator.
Not every connector supports virtual networks.
Plan subnet size and network policies before you start.
vnet-private-connectivity.dataNote: Calls to protected resources stay on your private network instead of the public internet.

learn.title: Configure Virtual Network support for outbound connections from agents
Microsoft Azure VNet support overview

cc-voice-settings.definition: Voice settings shape how an agent sounds and listens on phone calls, such as its voice, when a caller has finished speaking, and silence.

blocks.label: Voice
blocks.plain: The speaking voice, speed, and pitch, or a built-in voice.

blocks.label: Touch-tone input
blocks.plain: Callers can press keys; a timeout and an end key mark the entry done.

blocks.label: Turn-taking
blocks.plain: Settings decide when the agent thinks a caller has finished speaking.

blocks.label: Silence
blocks.plain: Silence detection is off by default; without it, the agent waits.

blocks.label: Delay message
blocks.plain: A message can play while the agent works; this applies to phone channels.

flow.label: Greet
flow.plain: A call connects, and the agent speaks in its configured voice.

flow.label: Listen
flow.plain: The agent listens and decides when the caller has finished.

flow.label: Keypad
flow.plain: Callers can also key in numbers when that is allowed.

flow.label: Wait
flow.plain: If the caller is silent, the agent follows up, if silence detection is on.

flow.label: Bridge
flow.plain: During a long wait, a short message can play.

example.input: A caller pauses mid-sentence to find an account number.
example.output: A longer wait before the agent speaks helps stop it from cutting in while the caller is still thinking.

whenToUse: Tune how natural a phone call feels.
Match listening settings to noisy or quiet places.
Handle callers who stay silent.
whenNot: Sub-agents inherit the primary agent's voice settings; set them once.
Test timeouts with real calls; short waits can cut callers off.
Delay messages apply only to phone channels.

learn.title: Configure voice settings (Customer Conversation)
Speech and chat settings overview (Customer Conversation)

cc-events.definition: Conversation events are built-in topics for key moments, such as the start, the end, and errors, that you can edit but not remove.

blocks.label: Start and end
blocks.plain: Events for the greeting and the end of the conversation.

blocks.label: Error and silence
blocks.plain: Events for errors and for silence on a call.

blocks.label: Reset
blocks.plain: An event defines the commands that start a new conversation.

blocks.label: Sign-in prompt
blocks.plain: A chat-only event customizes the text of the sign-in button.

blocks.label: Voice sign-in
blocks.plain: Three more events appear when voice authentication is on.

flow.label: Begin
flow.plain: The conversation starts, and the start event runs.

flow.label: Greet
flow.plain: The event greets the person and can load details such as a phone number.

flow.label: Talk
flow.plain: The AI-driven conversation fills the middle.

flow.label: Problem
flow.plain: If something goes wrong, the error event runs.

flow.label: End
flow.plain: A redirect to the end event closes the conversation, with survey logic.

example.input: A caller reaches a Contoso agent through a contact center.
example.output: The start event greets the caller and can load the phone number passed from the contact center.

whenToUse: Make key moments predictable around the AI-driven middle.
Customize greetings, endings, and survey logic.
Set up error logging.
whenNot: You cannot remove events; you can only disable and edit them.
The sign-in prompt event applies only to chat channels.

learn.title: Events overview (Customer Conversation)

prompt-tools.definition: A prompt tool is a saved, single-turn AI instruction that an agent can run as a tool.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: What the model should do, written clearly and specifically.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Values the prompt receives each time, such as text or an image.

blocks.label: Settings
blocks.plain: The model, temperature, knowledge, and output format for the prompt.

blocks.label: Testing
blocks.plain: Sample inputs let you test the prompt before you save it.

blocks.label: As a tool
blocks.plain: The agent decides when to run the prompt, from its description.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for a focused task, such as a summary.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The agent picks the prompt tool by its name and description.

flow.label: Fill
flow.plain: It supplies the inputs the prompt expects.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The model runs the prompt once and returns its result.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent uses the result in its answer.

example.input: A Contoso help agent needs a short summary of a ticket history.
example.output: The agent runs the saved summary prompt on the history and uses the result in its reply.

whenToUse: Package one focused AI task so you can test and reuse it.
Return output in a set format.
Keep one task out of the agent's general instructions.
whenNot: A prompt is single-turn; it cannot hold a back-and-forth.
The Microsoft Copilot harness does not support prompt tools; it uses skills.
Prompts are limited to certain regions and may be throttled.
prompt-tools.dataNote: Agents that allow anonymous users cannot use Dataverse tables as prompt knowledge.

learn.title: Use prompts to make your agent or agent flow perform specific tasks
Add tools to custom agents

cc-escalate-human.definition: Escalation hands a chat to a person when the agent cannot solve the problem, by phone, email, or live agent.

blocks.label: Escalate tool
blocks.plain: A prebuilt tool that gives the agent built-in handoff paths.

blocks.label: Teams Phone
blocks.plain: Hands the caller to a person by phone.

blocks.label: Email
blocks.plain: Hands the matter off by email.

blocks.label: Customer Engagement
blocks.plain: Sends the whole conversation to the engagement hub, which finds a live agent.

blocks.label: Per sub-agent
blocks.plain: Each sub-agent can have its own escalation path.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: A customer talks with the agent about an issue.

flow.label: Trigger
flow.plain: The customer asks for a live agent, or the instructions detect a need.

flow.label: Hand off
flow.plain: The agent uses the escalation path set for it.

flow.label: Send
flow.plain: With Customer Engagement, the full chat goes to the engagement hub.

flow.label: Pick up
flow.plain: A live agent picks up with full context.

example.input: A Contoso customer says, 'I want to talk to a person.'
example.output: The agent uses its escalation path, and a live agent can pick up the conversation with full context.

whenToUse: Customers must be able to reach a person.
Different specialists need different queues.
Hard issues should not leave the customer stuck.
whenNot: Only the Customer Engagement path is said to send the full chat.
It is a tool for the Customer Conversation harness.
cc-escalate-human.dataNote: With Customer Engagement, the agent sends the full chat to the engagement hub.

learn.title: Prebuilt contact center tools (Customer Conversation)

cc-model-mode.definition: The model mode sets how the agent's AI trades cost against speed: one mode favors cost for chat, and one favors low delay for voice.

blocks.label: Cost mode
blocks.plain: Auto, optimized for cost, uses a text model; it suits chat.

blocks.label: Latency mode
blocks.plain: Auto, optimized for latency, uses a speech-to-speech model; it suits voice.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.plain: The mode on the primary agent applies to all its sub-agents.

blocks.label: Connected agents
blocks.plain: A connected Foundry agent uses a model chosen in Foundry.

blocks.label: Admin limits
blocks.plain: Administrators control preview and experimental models.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: The maker decides whether the agent mostly chats or takes calls.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: A mode is set once on the primary agent.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: The primary agent and all sub-agents use that mode.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: Chat uses the text model, and voice can use the speech model.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The team tests response time, because the model affects how long the agent takes.

example.input: A Contoso help line answers mostly phone calls.
example.output: The latency-optimized mode fits, because voice and real-time scenarios need quick responses.

whenToUse: Phone and real-time scenarios need low delay.
Chat and text-first scenarios can favor cost.
Set one mode for the whole agent team.
whenNot: Preview and experimental models are not for production.
A connected Foundry agent needs its own model choice.
cc-model-mode.dataNote: Some models use cross-geography processing, so data may be handled outside your region.

learn.title: Select a model for an agent (Customer Conversation)

computer-use.definition: Computer use lets an agent use a website or desktop app by its screen, like a person, when no direct link exists.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Plain-language steps that name the exact sites or apps to use.

blocks.label: Machine
blocks.plain: A configured computer where the tool runs.

blocks.label: Credentials
blocks.plain: Maker credentials by default, or the end user's.

blocks.label: Guardrails
blocks.plain: An allow list, secure sites only, and human review reduce risk.

blocks.label: Credits
blocks.plain: Each step uses 5 Copilot Credits, or 15 for a premium model.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: A person asks, or an event starts, a task with no direct connection.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: The tool reads its instructions and looks at the screen.

flow.label: Act
flow.plain: It clicks, selects, and types on the configured machine.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: If it spots harmful instructions, it can ask a person to review.

flow.label: Finish
flow.plain: It returns the result, such as extracted text, to the agent.

example.input: A Contoso clerk needs invoice details copied from a PDF into a web form that has no connector.
example.output: Computer use reads the PDF and fills in the form on a set-up machine, using AI vision.

whenToUse: No connector or direct link exists, but a person could do the task.
Data entry, invoice handling, or data extraction.
Background tasks run by autonomous agents.
whenNot: It works only for agents that have generative orchestration turned on.
Anyone using a shared agent could act with the maker's access on that machine.
On the Microsoft Copilot harness, computer use is planned, not available.
computer-use.dataNote: Stored passwords are encrypted in Power Platform storage or kept in your own Azure Key Vault. Screenshots and reasoning can appear in the chat.

learn.title: Automate web and desktop apps with computer use

agent-to-agent.definition: Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open standard that lets Copilot Studio send a task to an outside agent, along with details about that agent.

blocks.label: A2A agent
blocks.plain: An agent hosted outside Copilot Studio that follows the A2A standard.

blocks.label: Endpoint
blocks.plain: Use the agent's communication address, not its agent card address.

blocks.label: Agent card
blocks.plain: A file where a valid agent can publish its name and description.

blocks.label: Authentication
blocks.plain: None, a key, or OAuth 2.0, depending on the agent.

blocks.label: Your duty
blocks.plain: You review and test outside agents, including data handling and oversight.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for something an outside agent specializes in.

flow.label: Route
flow.plain: Copilot Studio matches the request to the agent's name and description.

flow.label: Send
flow.plain: It sends the task, with rich details and the chat history, over A2A.

flow.label: Work
flow.plain: The outside agent does the work with its own reasoning.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: It sends back a reply in a predictable format, and the agent answers.

example.input: A Contoso garden-store agent is asked which plant needs more light, a tomato or a strawberry.
example.output: The agent delegates the question to a connected A2A plant-care agent and shows its reply.

whenToUse: The other agent already supports the A2A standard.
It is built on another framework or hosted elsewhere.
You need multi-turn exchange with rich details, not a basic web call.
whenNot: For plain web services, use a custom connector or web tool instead.
Agents built with a software development kit (SDK) use their own connection path.
You are responsible for the data and safety of outside agents.
agent-to-agent.dataNote: A2A messages can include the full chat history, so decide what data an outside agent may receive.

learn.title: Connect an agent available over the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol

flow-async.definition: Asynchronous response lets a long agent flow keep working past two minutes and call back with its result.

blocks.label: Normal limit
blocks.plain: A flow that answers in real time has a short time limit.

blocks.label: Async mode
blocks.plain: A setting lets the flow keep running and respond later.

blocks.label: Callback
blocks.plain: When the flow finishes, it sends its result back to the agent.

blocks.label: Channels
blocks.plain: Callbacks work fully in Teams, but not in Microsoft Copilot or phone channels.

blocks.label: Environment
blocks.plain: Only environments on the new infrastructure support it.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for something that takes a long time.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: The agent starts the flow.

flow.label: Continue
flow.plain: If the person sends another message, the agent answers it without waiting.

flow.label: Finish
flow.plain: The flow completes after more than two minutes and calls back.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: The agent shares the result when the callback arrives.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks for a large report that takes several minutes to build.
example.output: The flow keeps running and then calls back, so the agent can share the result when it is done.

whenToUse: Work takes longer than the normal response window.
The person can keep chatting while it runs.
The channel is Teams, where callbacks are fully supported.
whenNot: If the agent must answer at once, remove the reply step instead.
Phone and Microsoft Copilot channels do not support callbacks.
Environments on older infrastructure do not support it.

learn.title: Asynchronous response support for agent flows

adaptive-cards.definition: An Adaptive Card is a small card of text, images, and buttons that shows information or collects answers inside a chat.

blocks.label: Card
blocks.plain: Text, images, buttons, and input fields in one layout.

blocks.label: Message or card
blocks.plain: Display-only cards go in messages; cards that collect answers use a card step.

blocks.label: Variables
blocks.plain: Answers from the card are saved in variables.

blocks.label: Dynamic values
blocks.plain: A Power Fx formula can fill the card with live values.

blocks.label: Versions
blocks.plain: Copilot Studio supports card version 1.6 and earlier; channels may support less.

flow.label: Reach
flow.plain: The conversation reaches a step that shows a card.

flow.label: Show
flow.plain: The person sees text, images, buttons, or fields.

flow.label: Submit
flow.plain: The person fills in the fields and sends the card.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: The answers are saved in variables.

flow.label: Continue
flow.plain: If the reply is invalid, the agent asks again, up to two times by default.

example.input: A Contoso customer must give a name before a booking.
example.output: The agent shows a card with a name field and a submit button, then saves the name in a variable.

whenToUse: Collect several details at once in a form.
Present results with buttons for the next action.
Show text and images in a layout that is easy to scan.
whenNot: Some channels render fewer card versions; Teams supports up to 1.5.
Older cards can be submitted again, so mark each submit action clearly.
Instructions cannot change when a card appears.

learn.title: Ask questions with Adaptive Cards

power-fx.definition: Power Fx is a low-code formula language, like Excel, that sets values and tests conditions in a conversation.

blocks.label: Formula
blocks.plain: An Excel-like expression that works out a value.

blocks.label: Variable scope
blocks.plain: Name the scope first: Topic, Global, System, or Environment.

blocks.label: Conditions
blocks.plain: A formula can decide which path a conversation takes.

blocks.label: Data work
blocks.plain: It can parse text, work with dates, and handle tables.

blocks.label: Format
blocks.plain: Formulas use US-style numbers and commas between parts.

flow.label: Collect
flow.plain: The conversation gathers values, such as a name or a date.

flow.label: Compute
flow.plain: A formula calculates a new value from those variables.

flow.label: Store
flow.plain: The result is saved in a variable.

flow.label: Branch
flow.plain: A condition uses the result to pick the next path.

flow.label: Show
flow.plain: A message or card uses the result.

example.input: A customer gives a booking date.
example.output: A formula checks whether the date is 14 or more days away, and the agent says whether a discount applies.

whenToUse: Use exact rules for text, dates, and numbers.
Branch on a condition that needs a real calculation.
Fill a card with live values.
whenNot: Put the scope prefix on each variable, or the formula will not find it.
Formulas use commas, not semicolons, between parts.

learn.title: Create expressions using Power Fx

entities-variables.definition: Entities pick details out of what people say, and variables store those details so later steps can use them.

blocks.label: Entity
blocks.plain: A kind of detail, such as money, a date, or a name.

blocks.label: Prebuilt
blocks.plain: Ready-made entities cover common types like numbers and cities.

blocks.label: Custom
blocks.plain: Closed lists with synonyms, or text patterns, for your own terms.

blocks.label: Variable
blocks.plain: A named value that holds the answer.

blocks.label: Slot filling
blocks.plain: The agent can fill several details from one message.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A question step asks for a detail.

flow.label: Detect
flow.plain: The agent finds the detail, using the entity type.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: The value is saved in a variable.

flow.label: Reuse
flow.plain: Later steps and other topics can use it.

flow.label: Skip
flow.plain: If the person already gave the detail, the agent can skip the question.

example.input: A customer says, 'I want to book a hike in Seattle next Friday.'
example.output: The agent can pick out the activity, city, and date and fill them in at once, instead of asking three questions.

whenToUse: Turn free text into values that tools can use.
Avoid asking for the same information twice.
Use closed lists for domain terms that have synonyms.
whenNot: Custom entities cannot yet be tool or topic inputs; use a question step.
Closed lists suit small, simple lists that are easy to manage.

learn.title: Use entities and slot filling in agents
Work with variables

cc-skills.definition: On the Customer Conversation harness, a skill is either a generative skill the agent reasons over, or a topic skill with fixed steps.

blocks.label: Generative skill
blocks.plain: Instructions the agent reasons over in the moment.

blocks.label: Topic skill
blocks.plain: A fixed, authored flow of steps and conditions.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: A short name, plus a description of up to 200 characters that guides routing.

blocks.label: Size
blocks.plain: Aim for about 3,000 characters per skill and at most 10 per sub-agent.

flow.label: Request
flow.plain: A customer asks for something a skill covers.

flow.label: Match
flow.plain: The orchestrator matches the request to a skill's description.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: A generative skill guides the agent; a topic skill runs fixed steps.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent answers the customer with the result.

example.input: A Contoso customer asks to look up an order.
example.output: An order-lookup skill guides the agent, or a topic skill runs fixed steps, depending on how it was built.

whenToUse: Generative skill: flexible handling of a scenario.
Topic skill: exact, repeatable logic.
Give each sub-agent only the skills it needs.
whenNot: Long skills crowd out conversation history.
A skill gives instructions, not a connection to a service.

learn.title: Create a skill for an agent (Customer Conversation)

model-selection.definition: On the standard harness, you pick the primary AI model for an agent by weighing speed, quality, reasoning, and cost.

blocks.label: General
blocks.plain: Fast and low cost; good for everyday chat and light grounding.

blocks.label: Auto
blocks.plain: Adapts to each turn; good for mixed workloads.

blocks.label: Deep
blocks.plain: Slowest and costliest; best for multistep reasoning.

blocks.label: Default
blocks.plain: The default model is a fallback if another is turned off or unavailable.

blocks.label: Release types
blocks.plain: Experimental and preview models are for testing only.

flow.label: Weigh
flow.plain: Compare what the agent needs: speed, quality, reasoning, and cost.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The maker picks a primary model for the agent.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: That model powers generative orchestration.

flow.label: Fall back
flow.plain: If the model is unavailable, the default model steps in.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with real questions before release.

example.input: A Contoso agent mostly answers quick FAQ questions.
example.output: A general model fits, because it favors speed and low cost for everyday grounded answers.

whenToUse: Match the model to the job.
Use a deep model for complex, multistep work.
Keep the default for most scenarios.
whenNot: Do not use experimental or preview models in production.
Deep models are the slowest and cost the most.
model-selection.dataNote: Data sent to an experimental model might be handled outside your region.

learn.title: Select a primary AI model for your agent

vscode-authoring.definition: The Visual Studio Code extension lets developers clone an agent to local files, edit it, and sync changes with Copilot Studio.

blocks.label: Clone
blocks.plain: Downloads the agent's definition and parts to a local folder.

blocks.label: Edit
blocks.plain: Change topics, tools, and knowledge files as text, with code help.

blocks.label: Sync
blocks.plain: Preview, get, and apply changes between local files and the cloud.

blocks.label: Apply
blocks.plain: Applying updates the agent but does not publish it.

blocks.label: Teamwork
blocks.plain: Git history and pull requests work as they do for code.

flow.label: Clone
flow.plain: A developer downloads the agent to local files.

flow.label: Edit
flow.plain: They change the files with normal editor tools.

flow.label: Preview
flow.plain: They check for remote changes first.

flow.label: Apply
flow.plain: They upload their changes to the agent.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The team tests in Copilot Studio, then publishes when ready.

example.input: Two Contoso developers want to review each other's agent changes.
example.output: They keep the agent files in Git and review the changes in a pull request before applying them.

whenToUse: You want version control and reviews for agents.
Large agents are easier to manage as text.
You want coding assistants to help update agent files.
whenNot: Applying changes the live agent right away, so review first.
You cannot apply while unseen remote changes exist; get them first.
It is aimed at developers; makers can use the web designer.

learn.title: Overview of the Microsoft Copilot Studio extension for Microsoft Visual Studio Code
Synchronize your changes

channel-web-sdk.definition: The Microsoft 365 Agents software development kit (SDK) lets your own web or native app talk to a published agent.

blocks.label: Client library
blocks.plain: Code your app uses to send and receive agent messages.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: A connection string or agent details point the app at the agent.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: The app signs people in; this is separate from the agent's own sign-in rule.

blocks.label: Ready-made embed
blocks.plain: A no-code chat embed exists for agents that need no sign-in.

blocks.label: Direct Line
blocks.plain: Another route for cases the kit does not cover.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The agent is published and ready to be called.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The app is pointed at the agent with its connection details.

flow.label: Send
flow.plain: The app sends the person's message to the agent.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The agent answers through the same connection.

flow.label: Show
flow.plain: The app shows the reply in its own design.

example.input: A Contoso mobile app wants its own chat screen for the help agent.
example.output: The app uses the client library to send messages to the published agent and shows the replies in its own design.

whenToUse: You want your own look and sign-in model.
Your app already has client code and users.
You need to send context from the app to the agent.
whenNot: For a simple public chat box, use the ready-made embed.
The ready-made embed lets anyone with the link chat, with no sign-in.
Do not turn off sign-in just to test an app connection.

learn.title: Integrate web or native apps with Microsoft 365 Agents SDK

mc-sdk-agent.definition: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, you can connect an agent built in code, so the primary agent can hand it tasks.

blocks.label: Messaging endpoint
blocks.plain: The web address where the code agent accepts messages.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: You supply them, because this agent publishes no agent card.

blocks.label: Authentication
blocks.plain: None, a key, or OAuth 2.0; a key is stored with the connection.

blocks.label: Routing
blocks.plain: The primary agent routes by name, description, and your instructions.

blocks.label: Your duty
blocks.plain: You review and test the agent, including data flows and oversight.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: Developers build the agent in code and host it.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker enters its address, name, description, and sign-in details.

flow.label: Route
flow.plain: The primary agent delegates when a request fits its description.

flow.label: Work
flow.plain: The code agent handles the task.

flow.label: Reply
flow.plain: The primary agent shares the result with the person.

example.input: Contoso developers built a code agent that checks warranty status.
example.output: The primary agent hands warranty questions to it, based on the name and description the maker supplied.

whenToUse: A developer team already built an agent in code.
You want a primary agent to delegate to code-built specialists.
whenNot: Without an agent card, names and descriptions must be written by hand.
Delegation goes one level deep.
You must review and test outside agents yourself.
mc-sdk-agent.dataNote: You are responsible for how data flows to and from an agent hosted outside Copilot Studio.

learn.title: Add a Microsoft 365 Agents SDK agent as a connected agent (Microsoft Copilot)

custom-connectors.definition: A custom connector wraps your own service so agents, flows, and apps can call its operations like any other connector.

blocks.label: Your service
blocks.plain: A web service you own or can reach.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.plain: A machine-readable description of the service's operations.

blocks.label: Security
blocks.plain: You pick a sign-in method; Microsoft Entra ID is recommended.

blocks.label: Sharing
blocks.plain: Share it in your organization, or certify it to share widely.

blocks.label: Connections
blocks.plain: People create connections to call its operations.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: A team builds or picks the service the connector will wrap.

flow.label: Secure
flow.plain: The service is protected with a standard sign-in method.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: The service's operations are described to the connector.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: Agents call it like a ready-made connector tool.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: It can be shared with others in the organization.

example.input: Contoso wants its agent to call an internal order service that has no ready-made connector.
example.output: A custom connector exposes approved operations as tools, with sign-in handled by the connector.

whenToUse: No ready-made connector exists for your service.
You want one place to manage sign-in settings.
Share approved operations across apps, flows, and agents.
whenNot: Over 1,000 ready-made connectors exist; check them first.
To use it in an agent, share it across your organization.

learn.title: Custom connectors overview
Add tools to custom agents

fdy-create-prompt-agent.definition: A prompt agent is a Foundry agent you define with a model, instructions, and tools, and that runs on the Foundry service.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.plain: A model from the Foundry model catalog that you have deployed.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Plain-language rules that define how the agent behaves.

blocks.label: Tools
blocks.plain: Optional tools the agent can call, such as file search.

blocks.label: Versions
blocks.plain: You can create new versions and update or delete the agent anytime.

blocks.label: Project
blocks.plain: The agent lives in a Foundry project with a model and tracing ready.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: A team deploys a model and connects tracing in a Foundry project.

flow.label: Define
flow.plain: A developer defines the agent with a model and instructions.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: Foundry saves it as a named agent.

flow.label: Chat
flow.plain: A person asks a question, then a related follow-up.

flow.label: Remember
flow.plain: The conversation keeps its history across both turns.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants a simple help agent without writing hosting code.
example.output: They define a prompt agent with a model and instructions, then chat with it and ask a follow-up question.

whenToUse: You can describe the agent with a model and instructions alone.
You want the agent to run on the Foundry service, not your own server.
You may add tools such as file search later.
whenNot: A prompt agent follows a definition; hosted agents run your own code.
The quickstart code needs Azure AI Projects 2.x; version 1.x does not work.
Spoken voice conversations have their own voice-based prompt agent.
fdy-create-prompt-agent.needToKnow: A prompt agent is defined by a model, instructions, and optional tools rather than by your own code. The quickstart needs a deployed model and tracing connected to the project. Chat history carries across a question and its follow-up.
fdy-create-prompt-agent.demo: Show the agent definition on one slide, then chat with the agent and ask a follow-up that depends on its first answer.
fdy-create-prompt-agent.askTheRoom: What simple helper could you describe with a model and one paragraph of instructions?
fdy-create-prompt-agent.sayOutLoud: A prompt agent is like a job description that Foundry carries out for you. At Contoso, a developer writes the rules once, and people can then chat with the agent.

quiz.q: What defines a prompt agent?
options: A model, instructions, and optional tools
A web server you build and host
quiz.why: A prompt agent is declaratively defined. It combines a model, instructions, tools, and prompts.

quiz.q: What does the quickstart need before you create the agent?
options: A model deployed in your project
quiz.why: The prerequisites list a model deployed in Foundry and tracing connected to the project.

quiz.q: What does the conversation keep across turns?
quiz.why: Learn says the conversation maintains history across a question and a related follow-up.

quiz.q: When would you choose a hosted agent instead?
options: When you need to run your own code
quiz.why: Hosted agents run code you write. A prompt agent is defined by a model, instructions, and tools.

learn.title: Quickstart: Create a prompt agent

fdy-agent-file-search.definition: File search lets a Foundry agent answer from your own documents by searching a store that holds those files.

blocks.label: Files
blocks.plain: Your own documents, such as PDFs and Word files.

blocks.label: Vector store
blocks.plain: A search store the files go into; it supports keyword and meaning searches.

blocks.label: File search tool
blocks.plain: The tool you give the agent so it can look in the store.

blocks.label: Setup type
blocks.plain: Standard keeps files in your own storage; basic uses Microsoft's storage.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Files up to 512 megabytes; one store holds up to 10,000 files.

flow.label: Upload
flow.plain: A developer uploads a file and adds it to a vector store.

flow.label: Ingest
flow.plain: The service reads and prepares the file so it can be searched.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks a question that only the file can answer.

flow.label: Search
flow.plain: The tool rewrites the query, searches by keyword and meaning, and ranks results.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The agent writes an answer grounded in the passages it found.

example.input: A Contoso agent is asked about a fact that appears only in an uploaded manual.
example.output: File search finds the passage in the manual, and the agent answers from it instead of from general model knowledge.

whenToUse: Search documents you upload, such as PDFs and Word files.
Answer from proprietary or confidential content.
Handle files up to 512 megabytes without running your own search.
whenNot: To search an existing search index, use the Azure AI Search tool.
For current information from the public web, use the web search tool.
File search has extra charges beyond model token fees.
fdy-agent-file-search.dataNote: With standard setup, your files stay in your own storage and your own search resource ingests them. In a hosted agent that uses a toolbox, everyone in the project shares access to the referenced stores.
fdy-agent-file-search.needToKnow: File search grounds an agent in documents you upload. Wait until ingestion finishes, then test with a fact only your file contains. An agent can have at most one vector store attached.
fdy-agent-file-search.demo: Upload a short file with an unusual fact, ask the agent about it, and show the answer coming from the file.
fdy-agent-file-search.askTheRoom: Which documents would your team want an agent to answer from, and who may see them?
fdy-agent-file-search.sayOutLoud: File search is like handing the agent a binder. At Contoso, the agent can answer from the product manual you gave it, and not from guesses.

quiz.q: What does file search let an agent do?
options: Answer from your own uploaded files
quiz.why: File search grounds Foundry agents in your own data by retrieving from your documents.

quiz.q: What is a vector store?
options: A search store that holds your files
quiz.why: Adding a file to a vector store lets the tool search it by keywords and by meaning.

quiz.q: With the standard setup, where do your files stay?
quiz.why: Learn says the standard setup keeps files in your own storage, ingested by your own search resource.

quiz.q: What is a good test that file search works?
options: Ask a question only your file can answer
quiz.why: A fact only your file contains proves the answer came from the file.

learn.title: File search tool for agents
What is Toolbox in Foundry?

fdy-agent-ai-search.definition: The Azure AI Search tool lets a Foundry agent answer from one search index and show inline citations to its sources.

blocks.label: Search index
blocks.plain: A prepared copy of your content with searchable text and vector fields.

blocks.label: Citation fields
blocks.plain: A text field to cite and a source address field give link citations.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: A link between your Foundry project and the search service.

blocks.label: Keyless sign-in
blocks.plain: A managed identity with two search roles replaces keys.

blocks.label: Tool settings
blocks.plain: Index name, number of results (default 5), and query type.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The project is connected to the search service.

flow.label: Attach
flow.plain: The agent gets the search tool and one index name.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks a question that the index can answer.

flow.label: Retrieve
flow.plain: The tool pulls matching documents from the index.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The model writes an answer with inline citations.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: A tester confirms the cited content matches the source.

example.input: A person asks a Contoso product agent for a product's temperature rating.
example.output: The tool searches the product index, and the agent answers with a citation that links to the source document.

whenToUse: Your content already lives in a search index.
You want answers with inline citations.
You want to avoid hard-coded keys by using managed identity.
whenNot: The tool targets only one index.
The search service and the agent must be in the same tenant.
A basic agent setup does not support private search resources.
fdy-agent-ai-search.dataNote: If you use a private virtual network, the connection must use managed identity; keys are not supported.
fdy-agent-ai-search.needToKnow: The index needs text fields, vector fields, and a source address field before citations can link back. Keyless sign-in needs two roles on the search service for the Foundry account's identity. Remember the limits: one index per tool, one tenant, and no private resources on basic setup.
fdy-agent-ai-search.demo: Ask a question that one indexed document answers, and show the inline citation that points back to it.
fdy-agent-ai-search.askTheRoom: Where does your organization already keep searchable content that an agent could cite?
fdy-agent-ai-search.sayOutLoud: A search index is like a card catalog. At Contoso, the agent looks up the right card and tells you which card it used.

quiz.q: How many indexes can the tool target?
quiz.why: Learn lists a limit that the tool can only target one index.

quiz.q: Which sign-in method does a private virtual network require?
quiz.why: Key-based authentication is not supported with private virtual networking.

quiz.q: What helps citations show a link to the source?
options: A retrievable source address field in the index
quiz.why: The index needs a retrievable field with a source URL so citations can include a link.

learn.title: Connect a Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) index to Foundry agents
What is Toolbox in Foundry?

fdy-toolbox-tools.definition: A toolbox is a managed set of tools in Foundry that agents share through one endpoint that speaks Model Context Protocol (MCP).

blocks.label: Tools
blocks.plain: Web search, MCP servers, file search, search indexes, and more.

blocks.label: One endpoint
blocks.plain: Agents connect to one address and find every tool at run time.

blocks.label: Central control
blocks.plain: Sign-in, guardrails, and versions are managed in one place.

blocks.label: Tool search
blocks.plain: It finds the right tool when a toolbox holds many.

blocks.label: Versions
blocks.plain: A new version can be tested, then promoted to default.

flow.label: Define
flow.plain: A developer creates a toolbox version with a curated set of tools.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The first version becomes the default.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The developer checks that the expected tools load from the endpoint.

flow.label: Attach
flow.plain: An agent connects to the consumer endpoint.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: The agent finds and calls tools, and the toolbox handles credentials.

flow.label: Update
flow.plain: A promoted version reaches every agent without code changes.

example.input: Three Contoso agents need the same web search and an internal tool server.
example.output: One toolbox holds both tools, and all three agents connect to its single endpoint instead of wiring them separately.

whenToUse: Several agents need the same tools.
You want central credentials and guardrails.
A large tool set needs tool search.
whenNot: A toolbox allows only one unnamed tool of each built-in type; name the extras.
Non-Foundry tools can cost money and send data outside Foundry's compliance boundary.
Skills in a toolbox are in preview.
fdy-toolbox-tools.dataNote: Non-Foundry tools might send data outside Foundry's compliance boundary and process it under their own terms.
fdy-toolbox-tools.needToKnow: A toolbox defines tools once and exposes them through one endpoint that any MCP-compatible runtime can use. Give every tool a clear description so the model picks the right one. Grant the Foundry User role to the developer, to the agent identity for prompt agents, and to end users only for OAuth sign-in flows.
fdy-toolbox-tools.demo: Show one toolbox with two tools, then show two different agents loading the same tools from its endpoint.
fdy-toolbox-tools.askTheRoom: Which tools would your teams stop building twice if they could share them?
fdy-toolbox-tools.sayOutLoud: A toolbox is a shared tool shed. At Contoso, every agent borrows the same web search from one place, and the shed owner keeps the keys.

quiz.q: What does a toolbox give agents?
options: One endpoint to find shared tools
quiz.why: A toolbox exposes a curated set of tools through a single MCP-compatible endpoint.

quiz.q: What happens when you promote a toolbox version to default?
options: Agents that use the toolbox pick it up without code changes
quiz.why: Consumers connect to the endpoint that always serves the default version.

quiz.q: How many unnamed tools of the same built-in type can one toolbox hold?
quiz.why: A toolbox supports at most one tool of a type without a name. Give extras a unique name.

quiz.q: Why add a description to every tool?
options: It helps the model pick the right tool
It makes the tool run faster
quiz.why: Learn says a description on every tool helps the model select the right tool for each request.

learn.title: What is Toolbox in Foundry?
Create and manage a toolbox in Foundry

fdy-deploy-hosted-agent.definition: A hosted agent runs agent code that you write, which Foundry builds and deploys so people can call it through an endpoint.

blocks.label: Your code
blocks.plain: Code you write with a framework such as Microsoft Agent Framework or LangGraph.

blocks.label: Project setup
blocks.plain: A Foundry project, a deployed model, and tracing must be ready.

blocks.label: Command-line tool
blocks.plain: It sets up a sample, tests it locally, and deploys it.

blocks.label: Remote build
blocks.plain: Foundry builds the agent from your source and deploys it.

blocks.label: Cost
blocks.plain: Provisioning can create billable resources, so review them first.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: A developer creates the project from a sample agent.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: Azure resources named in the project file are created.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The agent runs locally, with an inspector to chat with it.

flow.label: Deploy
flow.plain: The source is packaged and uploaded, and Foundry builds and deploys it.

flow.label: Invoke
flow.plain: A test prompt confirms the deployed agent answers.

flow.label: Trace
flow.plain: Stored cloud traces confirm the first remote response.

example.input: A Contoso team outgrows a prompt agent and wants to run its own code.
example.output: They deploy a sample hosted agent, test it locally, deploy it to Foundry, and send it a test prompt.

whenToUse: You need your own code and framework.
You want to use a framework such as LangGraph.
You want Foundry to build and run your code.
whenNot: Review provisioning first; it can create resources that cost money.
You need specific roles, such as Foundry Project Manager on a project.
Cleanup can delete an entire resource group, so read the warning.
fdy-deploy-hosted-agent.needToKnow: A hosted agent is code you own, running on Foundry. Provisioning can create things the sample declares, such as a model deployment, so review them before you run it. Connect tracing before the first remote call.
fdy-deploy-hosted-agent.demo: Show a sample agent's files, run it locally, and then show the deployed agent answering the same test prompt.
fdy-deploy-hosted-agent.askTheRoom: What would your team build in code that a prompt agent could not do?
fdy-deploy-hosted-agent.sayOutLoud: A prompt agent is a recipe Foundry follows. A hosted agent is your own kitchen that Foundry runs for you. At Contoso, a team moves to the kitchen when the recipe stops being enough.

quiz.q: What is a hosted agent?
options: Agent code you write that Foundry builds and runs
quiz.why: Hosted agents support multiple frameworks. Foundry builds the agent remotely and deploys it.

quiz.q: What should you do before provisioning?
options: Review the resources the project file will create
quiz.why: Provisioning can create missing resources, such as a model deployment, and some can cost money.

quiz.q: Where do you test first?
quiz.why: The quickstart tests the agent locally, then deploys it and invokes it.

learn.title: Quickstart: Deploy your first hosted agent

fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.definition: A Foundry agent can be connected to a Copilot Studio agent, which hands it focused tasks that the Foundry agent answers.

blocks.label: Foundry agent
blocks.plain: A specialist agent made in the current Foundry portal.

blocks.label: Activity protocol
blocks.plain: It is off by default; without it, calls to the agent fail.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: It uses your Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and the project address.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: The orchestrator uses them to decide when to route.

blocks.label: Your duty
blocks.plain: You review and test connected agents that live outside Copilot Studio.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: The Foundry agent has the Activity protocol turned on.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker adds it as a connected agent with a name and description.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks the primary agent something in the Foundry agent's area.

flow.label: Route
flow.plain: The orchestrator matches the request to its name and description.

flow.label: Answer
flow.plain: The Foundry agent responds, and the primary agent shares the reply.

example.input: A Contoso front-door agent gets a request that a Foundry specialist agent handles.
example.output: The primary agent routes the request to the Foundry agent and then shows the reply to the person.

whenToUse: A specialist agent already lives in Foundry.
One front-door agent should route to specialists.
whenNot: Agents made in the previous Foundry portal return an error.
Without the Activity protocol, the connection is made but calls fail.
This article covers primary agents on the Microsoft Copilot harness, which uses Copilot Credits.
fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.dataNote: You own how data moves between agents, and you must review and test the setup.
fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.needToKnow: Copilot Studio talks to the Foundry agent over the Activity protocol, which is not on by default. Publishing a prompt agent to Microsoft 365 or Teams turns it on, or a developer can turn it on with a service call. The primary agent routes by name and description, so write them clearly.
fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.demo: Show the connected agent's name and description, then ask a question that is routed to it and one that is not.
fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.askTheRoom: Which specialist work already lives in Foundry that a front-door agent could use?
fdy-connect-agent-to-copilot-studio.sayOutLoud: The Foundry agent is a specialist down the hall. At Contoso, the front-door agent hears your question and walks it over to the right specialist.

quiz.q: Why must the Activity protocol be turned on?
options: Without it, the connection is made but calls fail
quiz.why: If the Activity protocol is not enabled, you can still add the connection, but calling the Foundry agent fails.

quiz.q: What does the primary agent use to route to the Foundry agent?
quiz.why: Routing uses the connected agent's name and description, the user's message, and the primary agent's instructions.

quiz.q: Which Foundry agents can you connect?
options: Agents made in the previous portal
Agents made in the current Foundry portal
quiz.why: Connecting to an agent made in the previous portal returns an error.

learn.title: Add a Foundry agent as a connected agent (Microsoft Copilot)

dca-agent-builder-first-agent.definition: Agent Builder is a no-code tool in Microsoft 365 Copilot where you describe an agent in plain language, then review and test it.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: You say in plain language what the agent should do.

blocks.label: Generated setup
blocks.plain: The tool fills in the name, instructions, and starter prompts.

blocks.label: Test chat
blocks.plain: A preview chat where you try the agent and refine it.

blocks.label: Built-in extras
blocks.plain: Code interpreter and image generator are available automatically.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Name up to 30 characters, description 1,000, instructions 8,000.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: A maker describes the agent in plain language.

flow.label: Generate
flow.plain: The tool fills in the name, description, instructions, and starter prompts.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The maker reviews the setup and adds knowledge sources.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tries the agent in the test chat.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The maker changes the agent by saying what to change.

example.input: A Contoso team lead wants an agent that summarizes the day's email.
example.output: They describe it in plain language, the tool adds their email as a knowledge source, and they test and refine it.

whenToUse: You want a no-code agent for Microsoft 365 Copilot.
You want to try an idea quickly.
Your agent needs knowledge and built-in capabilities, not outside actions.
whenNot: Agent Builder cannot author actions that call outside services.
Plain-language building works only in some languages; otherwise set it up by hand.
The test chat cannot share prompts or mention other agents.
dca-agent-builder-first-agent.needToKnow: Describing the agent in plain language is the recommended path, and it fills in the name, instructions, and starter prompts for you. You can also set everything up by hand. For actions that call outside services, copy the agent to Copilot Studio.
dca-agent-builder-first-agent.demo: Describe an agent in one sentence, show the setup the tool filled in, and ask the agent a question in the test chat.
dca-agent-builder-first-agent.askTheRoom: What small task would you hand to a helper agent first?
dca-agent-builder-first-agent.sayOutLoud: Agent Builder is like briefing a new assistant. You say what you need, the tool writes the job description, and you test the assistant right away.

quiz.q: What does Agent Builder need to get started?
options: A plain-language description of the agent
quiz.why: Learn recommends describing the agent in natural language, and Copilot builds it for you.

quiz.q: Which tools does every agent built here get automatically?
quiz.why: Learn says you automatically get the code interpreter and image generator capabilities.

quiz.q: What should you do if you need an action that calls an outside service?
options: Make a copy of the agent in Copilot Studio
quiz.why: Agent Builder does not support authoring actions that integrate external services, so Learn points to Copilot Studio.

quiz.q: What if plain-language building is not offered in your language?
quiz.why: Learn says you can configure the agent manually if natural language is not supported in your language.

learn.title: Build agents in Agent Builder

dca-agent-builder-templates-icon-mode.definition: A template is a ready-made starting point with a description, instructions, and prompts; you then add an icon and a default response mode.

blocks.label: Template
blocks.plain: A tested scaffold with a description, instructions, and prompts.

blocks.label: Customizing
blocks.plain: Use the template as it is, or change it and add knowledge.

blocks.label: Icon
blocks.plain: Make one with AI, pick one, or upload an image up to 1 megabyte.

blocks.label: Response mode
blocks.plain: Auto is the default; Quick response and Think deeper are the others.

blocks.label: User choice
blocks.plain: People using the agent can always change the response mode.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: A maker picks the template closest to the use case.

flow.label: Customize
flow.plain: The maker edits the description and instructions and adds knowledge.

flow.label: Icon
flow.plain: The maker adds an icon so the agent is easy to spot.

flow.label: Mode
flow.plain: The maker sets how deeply the agent thinks by default.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests the agent in the test chat.

example.input: A Contoso team picks a template that is close to what they need.
example.output: They tweak its instructions, add an icon, and keep the default mode, which weighs speed against depth for each question.

whenToUse: A template already matches your use case.
You want a tested scaffold, not a blank page.
You want a clear icon and a chosen default response mode.
whenNot: No template fits; describe the agent in plain language instead.
People can override the default mode, so it is not a strict control.
dca-agent-builder-templates-icon-mode.needToKnow: Templates arrive with a description, instructions, and prompts already filled in, and you can use them as they are or change them. The default response mode is Auto, with Quick response and Think deeper as the other choices. People using the agent can always override your choice.
dca-agent-builder-templates-icon-mode.demo: Show the template list, pick one, and point out its prefilled instructions. Then ask one question in two response modes.
dca-agent-builder-templates-icon-mode.askTheRoom: Which of your team's tasks sounds like something a template already covers?
dca-agent-builder-templates-icon-mode.sayOutLoud: A template is a form that is mostly filled in. You change what is different about your team, then give the agent an icon and decide how hard it thinks by default.

quiz.q: What does a template give you?
options: A description, instructions, and prompts already filled in
quiz.why: Learn says templates come preconfigured with a description, instructions, and prompts.

quiz.q: Which response mode is the default?
quiz.why: Auto is the default. The agent picks an approach that balances speed and depth.

quiz.q: Can people using the agent change the response mode?
options: Yes, they can always override it
quiz.why: Learn says users can always override the default response mode.

learn.title: Agent Builder templates
Build agents in Agent Builder

dca-write-agent-instructions.definition: Instructions are the rules you write for an agent: its job, its tone, and its steps. You improve them by testing.

blocks.label: Purpose
blocks.plain: Say what the agent is for and what role it plays.

blocks.label: Guidelines
blocks.plain: General directions, tone, and restrictions.

blocks.label: Knowledge and tools
blocks.plain: Name the sources and capabilities the agent should use.

blocks.label: Optional parts
blocks.plain: Steps, error handling, examples, and special terms.

blocks.label: Length limit
blocks.plain: Up to 8,000 characters, kept in the agent itself.

flow.label: Draft
flow.plain: A maker writes the purpose and the general guidelines.

flow.label: Structure
flow.plain: The maker uses clear verbs, short steps, and one task per step.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tries varied test prompts.

flow.label: Compare
flow.plain: The maker checks each answer against what was intended.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The maker edits the wording and tests again.

example.input: A Contoso agent answers in a different shape every time.
example.output: The maker adds a fixed output format and a tone rule, then tests again with the same prompts.

whenToUse: An agent gives uneven or off-topic answers.
You are writing instructions for the first time.
You want steady behavior as models change.
whenNot: Do not hide instructions in a file to beat the limit.
One long, tangled prompt is hard to test; keep each task small.
dca-write-agent-instructions.needToKnow: Good instructions state the agent's purpose and general guidelines, and may add steps, error handling, examples, and special terms. Use clear verbs and a strict structure, and say the tone, length, and output format you want. Copilot's models update automatically, so retest now and then.
dca-write-agent-instructions.demo: Show a vague instruction and a structured one side by side, then ask the agent the same question under each.
dca-write-agent-instructions.askTheRoom: What is one thing an assistant keeps getting wrong that a clear rule would fix?
dca-write-agent-instructions.sayOutLoud: Instructions are the agent's job description. Write them like a briefing for a new hire, with the purpose, the rules, and a sample of good work. Then test, because models can change over time.

quiz.q: Which belongs in good instructions?
options: The agent's purpose, guidelines, and expected tone
quiz.why: Learn lists purpose, general guidelines such as tone and restrictions, and the skills the agent uses.

quiz.q: Why retest instructions now and then?
options: Models update automatically, so behavior can shift
quiz.why: Learn notes that Copilot models are updated automatically, so wording that worked can behave differently.

quiz.q: Is it a good idea to keep instructions in a document to dodge the length limit?
options: Yes, if the file is a PDF
No, that content is not trusted and can be blocked
quiz.why: Learn warns against storing instructions in files to get around the limit.

quiz.q: What makes a step easier for the agent to follow?
options: Clear verbs and one task per step
quiz.why: Learn recommends clear verbs, a strict structure, and atomic tasks.

learn.title: Write effective instructions for declarative agents

dca-agent-builder-knowledge.definition: Knowledge sources are content an Agent Builder agent can search, so its answers come from your information.

blocks.label: Public websites
blocks.plain: Up to 4 web addresses, no more than two levels deep.

blocks.label: Work files
blocks.plain: Up to 100 SharePoint files, 50 OneDrive files, and one list.

blocks.label: Teams and email
blocks.plain: Up to 5 chats and 5 meetings; email cannot be narrowed.

blocks.label: Uploaded files
blocks.plain: Up to 20 files from your device become part of the agent.

blocks.label: Connectors
blocks.plain: Content from other systems, if an administrator turns connectors on.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: A maker picks the sources that hold the answers.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds them by description, link, search, or upload.

flow.label: Wait
flow.plain: New SharePoint and OneDrive files show a preparing status first.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: The maker asks a question only a source can answer.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The maker checks that the answer uses the expected information.

example.input: A Contoso HR team adds a policy site and asks about a rule only that site contains.
example.output: The answer uses the policy text, which shows the agent read the source and did not guess.

whenToUse: You want answers from specific content.
Your content lives in SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, or email.
You can stay within each source's limit.
whenNot: If Restricted SharePoint Search is on, SharePoint cannot be a source.
A list over 20,000 rows or 50 megabytes is cut off.
Teams and email depend on your license.
dca-agent-builder-knowledge.dataNote: The agent respects existing SharePoint and OneDrive permissions and sensitivity labels. Anyone who can use the agent sees answers grounded in uploaded files. People you share the agent with cannot use your email as knowledge.
dca-agent-builder-knowledge.needToKnow: Each source type has its own limit, so pick sources on purpose. New SharePoint and OneDrive files can show a preparing status for several minutes, and the agent does not use them until they are ready. Test with a question only your source can answer.
dca-agent-builder-knowledge.demo: Add one source, wait until it is ready, and ask a question that only that source can answer.
dca-agent-builder-knowledge.askTheRoom: Which three documents hold the answers people ask you for most?
dca-agent-builder-knowledge.sayOutLoud: Knowledge sources are the agent's bookshelf. Stock the shelf with your own content, and the agent reads from it to answer.

quiz.q: How many public website addresses can one agent use?
quiz.why: Learn lists a limit of four public website URLs for each agent.

quiz.q: Why might a new SharePoint file not show up in answers yet?
options: It can still be preparing for several minutes
quiz.why: New files can show a preparing status, and the agent does not use them until they are ready.

quiz.q: If you add a SharePoint site, are its lists included?
quiz.why: Selecting a site does not include its lists. To use a list, add that specific list.

quiz.q: What is a good test that a source works?
options: Ask a question only that source can answer
quiz.why: Learn says to ask a question whose answer is in a source and confirm the response uses it.

learn.title: Add knowledge sources to an agent in Agent Builder

dca-agent-builder-capabilities.definition: Code interpreter writes and runs Python code in a sandbox to analyze data and make charts or files. The image generator makes images from prompts.

blocks.label: Code interpreter
blocks.plain: Writes and runs Python to do math, analyze data, and draw charts.

blocks.label: Image generator
blocks.plain: Makes images from a prompt.

blocks.label: Sandbox
blocks.plain: The code runs in a protected space.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, CSV, and text files.

blocks.label: Outputs
blocks.plain: Charts, images, and files with a download link.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for a chart, a file, or an analysis.

flow.label: Write
flow.plain: The agent writes Python code for the task.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The code runs in the protected sandbox.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The agent returns a chart, an image, or a file to download.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The person checks the result against the data.

example.input: A Contoso analyst uploads a sales spreadsheet and asks for a chart of monthly totals.
example.output: The agent writes and runs code, then returns a chart and a file the analyst can download.

whenToUse: You need charts, math, or data analysis.
You want generated images or downloadable files.
Your people have a Microsoft 365 Copilot license.
whenNot: Generated files are kept only until the session ends.
Some Government clouds do not offer the image generator.
These capabilities cannot call outside services as actions.
dca-agent-builder-capabilities.dataNote: Files the agent makes are kept only until the session ends.
dca-agent-builder-capabilities.needToKnow: Both capabilities are available automatically to agents built in Agent Builder. Ask for a specific chart, file, or image, then check the result like any other work. Generated files are available only during the session, so download what you need.
dca-agent-builder-capabilities.demo: Upload a small spreadsheet, ask for a chart, and then ask for a simple generated image.
dca-agent-builder-capabilities.askTheRoom: Which report would you rather ask for in one sentence than build by hand?
dca-agent-builder-capabilities.sayOutLoud: Code interpreter is a calculator that writes its own formulas. Ask for a chart, and it writes the code, runs it, and hands you the file.

quiz.q: What does code interpreter run?
quiz.why: Learn says it writes and runs Python code in a sandboxed environment.

quiz.q: Which request suits code interpreter?
options: A chart from an uploaded spreadsheet
quiz.why: Learn lists graphs, data analysis, math, and downloadable files as supported uses.

quiz.q: How long are generated files hosted?
quiz.why: Files are hosted temporarily and are not kept after the session ends.

learn.title: Add the code interpreter capability to your agent
Build agents in Agent Builder

dca-agent-builder-skills.definition: A skill is a folder with steps and scripts for one task you repeat. The agent loads it only when it needs it.

blocks.label: Main file
blocks.plain: Holds the skill's name, description, and instructions.

blocks.label: Extra files
blocks.plain: Optional reference files and scripts in the same folder.

blocks.label: Ways to add
blocks.plain: Describe the skill in plain language, or upload a package.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Up to 8 skills per agent; a package up to 50 megabytes.

blocks.label: Sandbox
blocks.plain: Scripts run in a protected space with no network access.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: A maker describes the skill or uploads a skill package.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The skill is attached to the agent.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for the task the skill covers.

flow.label: Load
flow.plain: The agent loads the skill's contents only when the task needs them.

flow.label: Follow
flow.plain: The agent follows the skill's steps and may run its scripts.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The maker confirms the agent used the skill.

example.input: A Contoso team wants the same weekly report format every time.
example.output: They add a skill with the steps and a template, and the agent loads it whenever someone asks for that report.

whenToUse: A task must run the same way every time.
Your instructions are getting too long for one agent.
You want steps and scripts packaged together.
whenNot: Scripts have no network access and cannot call connectors or plugins.
Under Information Barriers, end users cannot add skills.
Packages are limited to 350 files in total and 25 megabytes per file.
dca-agent-builder-skills.dataNote: Skill files are stored in containers scoped to your tenant, and sensitivity labels are honored.
dca-agent-builder-skills.needToKnow: A skill packs repeatable instructions and scripts so a task runs the same way each time. An agent can hold up to 8 skills, and each loads only when the task needs it. Scripts run in a sandbox with no network access, so they cannot call other services.
dca-agent-builder-skills.demo: Add a small skill that sets a report format, then ask for that report and show the agent following it.
dca-agent-builder-skills.askTheRoom: What task does your team repeat the same way every week?
dca-agent-builder-skills.sayOutLoud: A skill is a recipe card in the agent's drawer. The agent pulls out the card only when the job calls for it, so the same job gets done the same way every time.

quiz.q: What is a skill?
options: A folder of instructions and optional scripts for one repeatable task
quiz.why: Learn describes a skill as a directory with a main file, plus optional files and scripts.

quiz.q: When does the agent load a skill's contents?
options: Only when the task needs them
quiz.why: Skills use progressive disclosure, so contents load only when the task needs them.

quiz.q: How many skills can one agent hold in Agent Builder?
quiz.why: Learn lists a limit of 8 skills per agent in Agent Builder.

quiz.q: Can skill scripts reach the internet?
options: No, the sandbox has no network access
quiz.why: Scripts run in a secure sandbox with no network access and cannot install packages.

learn.title: Add skills to your declarative agent in Agent Builder
Skills in declarative agents

dca-toolkit-typespec-agent.definition: In Visual Studio Code, you write the agent in a TypeSpec file, and Agents Toolkit builds the manifest from it.

blocks.label: Agents Toolkit
blocks.plain: A Visual Studio Code extension that builds and tests the agent.

blocks.label: TypeSpec file
blocks.plain: The source where you write the agent's name, instructions, and tools.

blocks.label: Manifest
blocks.plain: A generated file that Copilot reads to run the agent.

blocks.label: Provisioning
blocks.plain: It publishes the agent for testing and fails if custom app upload is blocked.

blocks.label: Copilot test
blocks.plain: You test the agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot.

flow.label: Scaffold
flow.plain: A developer creates a declarative agent project in the toolkit.

flow.label: Edit
flow.plain: The developer edits the TypeSpec file.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The toolkit turns the TypeSpec into the manifest.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The developer tests the agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot.

flow.label: Repeat
flow.plain: The developer changes the source and provisions again.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants the agent definition kept in source files.
example.output: They define the agent in TypeSpec, provision it, test it in Copilot, and keep the files with the rest of their code.

whenToUse: You want the agent defined in source files.
Your team already works in Visual Studio Code.
whenNot: For a no-code build, use Agent Builder instead.
Provisioning fails if your tenant blocks custom app upload.
Copilot Chat users get fewer features than licensed users.
dca-toolkit-typespec-agent.needToKnow: TypeSpec is the source you edit, and the manifest is the file the toolkit generates from it when you provision. Provisioning needs a tenant that allows custom app upload. The agent targets licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot users, and Copilot Chat users get limited capabilities.
dca-toolkit-typespec-agent.demo: Show the TypeSpec file, provision the agent, and ask it a question in Microsoft 365 Copilot.
dca-toolkit-typespec-agent.askTheRoom: Who on your team would rather keep an agent in code than in a form?
