dca-toolkit-typespec-agent.sayOutLoud: TypeSpec is the blueprint, and the manifest is the permit Copilot reads. You edit the blueprint, and the toolkit produces the permit when you provision.

quiz.q: What do you edit when you build an agent with TypeSpec?
quiz.why: You write the agent's instructions and capabilities in a TypeSpec file.

quiz.q: What does provisioning do with your TypeSpec?
options: Puts it into the agent's manifest
quiz.why: Learn says provisioning inserts the contents of the decorators into the agent's manifest.

quiz.q: What can make provisioning fail?
options: A tenant that does not allow custom app upload
quiz.why: Learn says provisioning fails if custom app upload is not enabled.

learn.title: Create declarative agents by using Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and TypeSpec

dca-toolkit-json-capabilities-action.definition: In the JSON route, you edit the agent file directly to add features and an action that calls a web service.

blocks.label: Manifest file
blocks.plain: A JSON file that lists the agent's instructions, capabilities, and actions.

blocks.label: Capabilities
blocks.plain: Built-in tools for charts, math, and images.

blocks.label: Schema version
blocks.plain: Code interpreter needs schema version 1.2 or newer.

blocks.label: Action
blocks.plain: An action that calls a web service described in an OpenAPI file.

blocks.label: Sample service
blocks.plain: The tutorial's action calls a free service that returns fake data.

flow.label: Scaffold
flow.plain: A developer creates a basic JSON agent project.

flow.label: Capabilities
flow.plain: The developer adds chart and image tools to the manifest.

flow.label: Action
flow.plain: The developer adds an action that uses an OpenAPI file.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The toolkit publishes the agent for testing.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The developer tests each tool and the action in Copilot.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants an agent that can chart data and read items from a sample service.
example.output: They add tools to the manifest and an action from an OpenAPI file, then test both.

whenToUse: You want to see how capabilities and actions are declared.
You prefer editing the manifest to writing TypeSpec.
whenNot: Government tenants cannot publish through the toolkit.
Some Government clouds do not support custom actions.
For a no-code agent, use Agent Builder instead.
dca-toolkit-json-capabilities-action.needToKnow: The manifest is plain JSON, so every capability and action you add is visible in one file. Code interpreter needs manifest schema version 1.2 or later. The tutorial's action calls a free sample service that returns fake data, so no real systems are touched.
dca-toolkit-json-capabilities-action.demo: Show the manifest before and after adding code interpreter, then ask for a chart in Copilot.
dca-toolkit-json-capabilities-action.askTheRoom: Which capability would you add first, and why?
dca-toolkit-json-capabilities-action.sayOutLoud: The manifest is the agent's spec sheet. Add a line for a capability, and the agent gains it. Add an action, and it can call a service.

quiz.q: What do you edit in the JSON route?
quiz.why: You add capabilities and actions directly in the declarative agent manifest.

quiz.q: What does code interpreter need in the manifest?
quiz.why: Learn says you must use version 1.2 or later of the manifest schema to add code interpreter.

quiz.q: What does the tutorial's action call?
options: A free sample service with fake data
quiz.why: The tutorial uses a free sample service that returns fake data.

learn.title: Tutorial: Create declarative agents by using Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and JSON
Add the code interpreter capability to your agent

dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.definition: Knowledge capabilities are settings that choose what the agent can read, such as the web, files, Teams, people, and email.

blocks.label: Capabilities
blocks.plain: Web, files, Teams messages, people, email, and Copilot connectors.

blocks.label: Scoping list
blocks.plain: Each capability can take a list that narrows what it reads.

blocks.label: No list
blocks.plain: Leave it out and the agent reaches all content the user can.

blocks.label: Email
blocks.plain: Can target specific folders or a shared mailbox.

blocks.label: Provisioning
blocks.plain: Each change takes effect after you provision again.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: A developer adds the settings the scenario needs.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: The developer adds lists of sites, folders, chats, or connections.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The toolkit updates the agent.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The developer asks questions and checks what the agent used.

flow.label: Tighten
flow.plain: The developer narrows any scope that reaches more than needed.

example.input: A Contoso support agent should read only the product support site and a shared support mailbox.
example.output: The developer lists that one site and mailbox, so the agent cannot reach other content the user can open.

whenToUse: The agent must read specific work content.
You want to limit what the agent can reach.
You want web, files, Teams, people, and email in one agent.
whenNot: A missing scoping list gives broad access to everything the user can reach.
For a no-code setup, use Agent Builder knowledge instead.
Copilot Chat users get fewer features than licensed users.
dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.dataNote: If you leave a list out, the agent can reach everything the signed-in user can, so scope each one on purpose.
dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.needToKnow: Each knowledge capability can take a list that limits it to certain sites, chats, folders, or connections. If you leave the list out, the agent can reach all content that the signed-in person can open. That makes scoping a security choice as well as a quality choice.
dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.demo: Add web search with one named site, then ask one question that needs that site and one that does not.
dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.askTheRoom: What is the narrowest set of content this agent really needs?
dca-toolkit-knowledge-capabilities.sayOutLoud: Think of a key ring. With no list, the agent holds the whole ring the user holds. A scoping list hands it only the keys it needs.

quiz.q: What happens if you leave a scoping list out?
options: The agent can reach all content the user can reach
quiz.why: Learn says that without the list, the agent can access all content the signed-in user can access.

quiz.q: How can email access be narrowed?
options: By listing specific folders or a shared mailbox
quiz.why: The email capability can limit access to folders, or point at a shared mailbox.

quiz.q: What does the web search capability use?
quiz.why: Learn says the web search capability lets agents use the search index in Bing.

learn.title: Create declarative agents by using Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit and TypeSpec

dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.definition: An application programming interface (API) plugin lets an agent read or change data in your web service.

blocks.label: Operations
blocks.plain: Each read, create, update, or delete call is declared in TypeSpec.

blocks.label: Descriptions
blocks.plain: Clear descriptions help Copilot pick the right operation.

blocks.label: Adaptive Card
blocks.plain: An optional card changes how results and citations look.

blocks.label: Not standalone
blocks.plain: The plugin works only inside the agent that contains it.

blocks.label: Hosting
blocks.plain: Your service is hosted outside Microsoft 365.

flow.label: Define
flow.plain: A developer sets the service address and its actions in TypeSpec.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The toolkit updates the agent with the action.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for something the action can do.

flow.label: Confirm
flow.plain: Copilot asks permission before first sending data to the service.

flow.label: Call
flow.plain: Copilot calls the right operation and shows the result.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants an agent to list, create, and update blog posts in a sample service.
example.output: They declare each operation in TypeSpec, provision the agent, and test each action with a plain prompt.

whenToUse: Your agent must read or change data in your own system.
You have a web service with an OpenAPI description.
You want results shown as cards.
whenNot: Agent Builder cannot author these actions.
Quality can drop when an agent has more than 10 functions or tools.
A plugin is not a standalone package that people install.
dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.dataNote: The service is hosted outside Microsoft 365. Copilot asks before first sending data to it, and asks again for calls that change data.
dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.needToKnow: An API plugin is an action, and it works only inside the agent that contains it. Good operation descriptions decide whether Copilot picks the right function, and quality can drop with more than about ten tools. Calls that change data ask for confirmation.
dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.demo: Show one read operation and one create operation in the TypeSpec file, then ask the agent to run each.
dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.askTheRoom: Which system of yours would you want an agent to read from first?
dca-toolkit-api-plugin-typespec.sayOutLoud: An API plugin is a phone line from the agent to your own system. The operation list is the menu of what the agent may ask for, and Copilot checks with the person before it sends data.

quiz.q: Can an API plugin work on its own, outside an agent?
options: No, it works inside a declarative agent
quiz.why: Learn says plugins provide actions within declarative agents and are not standalone installable packages.

quiz.q: What helps Copilot choose the right operation?
quiz.why: Learn says accurate descriptions let the orchestrator select the right action.

quiz.q: What does an Adaptive Card change?
options: How results and citations are shown
quiz.why: Learn says adding an Adaptive Card changes how citations in the response are rendered.

quiz.q: When does Copilot ask permission first?
options: Before first sending data to the plugin
quiz.why: Copilot asks the user before sending any data for the first time to a plugin.

learn.title: Build API plugins with TypeSpec for Microsoft 365 Copilot
MCP and API plugins for declarative agents

dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.definition: A Model Context Protocol (MCP) plugin connects a declarative agent to a remote MCP server so the agent can use that server's tools.

blocks.label: Remote server
blocks.plain: The plugin points to a running server and does not host it.

blocks.label: Sign-in choice
blocks.plain: OAuth with a saved client, OAuth with automatic registration, Entra sign-in, or none.

blocks.label: Return address
blocks.plain: The OAuth client must allow Teams' sign-in return address.

blocks.label: Dynamic tools
blocks.plain: By default the agent finds the server's current tools at run time.

blocks.label: Pinned tools
blocks.plain: You can pin a fixed set of tools instead.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: A developer sets up sign-in for the server.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The developer adds the server address and picks the sign-in type.

flow.label: Provision
flow.plain: The toolkit writes the manifest and publishes the agent for testing.

flow.label: Sign in
flow.plain: A person signs in through the agent the first time.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: The agent calls the server's tools to answer.

example.input: A Contoso developer follows Learn's example and connects a remote MCP server from GitHub.
example.output: They sign in through the agent and ask it to find a code repository.

whenToUse: A useful MCP server already exists.
You want new server tools without republishing the agent.
Each person must sign in to the server.
whenNot: Dynamic discovery lets tools change; pin tools if you need a fixed set.
Agents Toolkit version 6.12.0 or later is required.
Key-based sign-in is not supported for MCP plugins used as agent actions.
dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.dataNote: The server is hosted outside Microsoft 365. Copilot asks before first sending data to it.
dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.needToKnow: The plugin manifest points to a remote MCP server; it does not run the server. Pick the sign-in type your server supports, such as OAuth or Microsoft Entra sign-in. By default the agent finds the server's tools at run time, so new tools appear without republishing.
dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.demo: Show the server address and sign-in type in the toolkit, then sign in through the agent and ask a question that needs a server tool.
dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.askTheRoom: Which tool server does your company already run that an agent could use?
dca-toolkit-mcp-plugin.sayOutLoud: An MCP server is a tool shop that already exists. The plugin is a pointer, not a copy. It tells the agent where the shop is and how to sign in.

quiz.q: Does the MCP plugin host the server?
options: No, it connects to a remote server
quiz.why: Learn says the plugin manifest connects the agent to a remote MCP server and does not package or host it.

quiz.q: What is dynamic tool discovery?
options: A fixed list nobody can change
The agent finds the server's current tools at run time
quiz.why: By default Copilot resolves the plugin's tools at run time, directly from the MCP server.

quiz.q: Which sign-in type is not supported for MCP plugins used as agent actions?
quiz.why: Learn's support table lists key-based sign-in for the other plugin type, not for MCP plugins used as agent actions.

quiz.q: Which sign-in types can the toolkit set up for an MCP server?
options: OAuth, Microsoft Entra sign-in, or none
quiz.why: The toolkit offers OAuth with static or dynamic registration, Entra sign-in, or no authentication.

learn.title: Build a plugin for a declarative agent from an MCP server
MCP and API plugins for declarative agents

ppai-build-custom-prompt.definition: A custom prompt is a saved instruction for an AI model, with context and optional inputs, that you test first and reuse in apps, flows, and agents.

blocks.label: Instruction
blocks.plain: Clear directions for what the model should do.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.plain: The information the model needs to answer well.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Placeholders filled with new content each time the prompt runs.

blocks.label: Knowledge
blocks.plain: An optional data source, such as Dataverse.

blocks.label: Sample values
blocks.plain: They let you test the prompt before you save it.

flow.label: Write
flow.plain: A maker writes the instruction and the context.

flow.label: Inputs
flow.plain: The maker adds inputs for content that changes each run.

flow.label: Samples
flow.plain: The maker types a sample value for each input.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker runs the prompt and reads the response.

flow.label: Adjust
flow.plain: The maker makes the prompt more specific if the answer misses.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: The maker saves the prompt for reuse.

example.input: A Contoso team writes "Summarize this email in three bullets" and passes the email in as an input.
example.output: A sample email shows the three bullets, and the team tightens the wording until the response fits.

whenToUse: You need the same AI task again and again.
You want to test the response before wiring it in.
Apps, flows, or agents should share one prompt.
whenNot: Prompts are limited to some regions and may face usage limits.
Plan human review for results that matter.
ppai-build-custom-prompt.dataNote: If you add a knowledge object, the prompt can use your organization's data, such as Dataverse.
ppai-build-custom-prompt.needToKnow: A prompt has two parts: the instruction and the context. Good prompts are clear, specific, contextual, and relevant. Test with sample values first, and expect regional limits and possible usage limits.
ppai-build-custom-prompt.demo: Write a one-line instruction, add a sample input, run it, and then make the instruction more specific and run it again.
ppai-build-custom-prompt.askTheRoom: What small text task do you repeat that a saved prompt could handle?
ppai-build-custom-prompt.sayOutLoud: A prompt is a work order for the AI model. A good one says what to do and gives the background. Test it with sample content before anyone depends on it.

quiz.q: What are the two parts of a prompt?
quiz.why: Learn says a prompt generally has two parts: the instruction and the context.

quiz.q: Why add sample values to inputs?
options: To test the prompt before you save it
quiz.why: Sample values let you run the prompt and review the response before it is saved.

quiz.q: Which prompt is likely to give a more relevant answer?
options: A specific one with the topic and audience
quiz.why: Learn says a good prompt is clear, specific, contextual, and relevant.

learn.title: Create a prompt
Prompts overview

ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.definition: Inputs let one prompt handle new text or files each run. Model settings tune its speed, cost, and safety.

blocks.label: Inputs
blocks.plain: Text, an image or document, or a Power Fx formula.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.plain: Mini, General, and Deep models trade speed, depth, and cost.

blocks.label: Temperature
blocks.plain: A 0 to 1 slider; lower is steadier, higher is more varied.

blocks.label: Moderation
blocks.plain: Low, Moderate, or High; Moderate is the default.

blocks.label: File limits
blocks.plain: Files must total under 25 megabytes and under 50 pages.

flow.label: Inputs
flow.plain: A maker adds inputs for content that changes each run.

flow.label: Model
flow.plain: The maker picks a model that fits the task and the budget.

flow.label: Temperature
flow.plain: The maker sets how steady or varied answers should be.

flow.label: Safety
flow.plain: The maker sets the content moderation level.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with sample data and compares results.

example.input: A Contoso team's prompt summarizes a PDF, and the answers vary too much.
example.output: They lower the temperature so answers stay steady, then test again with the same sample file.

whenToUse: One prompt must handle different content each run.
Answers vary more than you want.
You need stricter or looser content filtering.
whenNot: Inputs cannot contain instructions; the service blocks them for security.
File input is not yet supported for prompts used as agent tools.
The moderation setting works only with managed models.
ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.dataNote: External models, such as Anthropic's, are hosted outside Microsoft and follow their own terms and data handling.
ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.needToKnow: Model categories are Mini, General, and Deep, and the default is a Mini model. Temperature runs from 0 to 1 and starts at 0, the most predictable setting. The content moderation level is Low, Moderate, or High, and Moderate is the default.
ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.demo: Run one prompt with a low temperature and again with a high temperature, and compare the answers side by side.
ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.askTheRoom: Where would a steadier answer matter more than a creative one in your work?
ppai-prompt-inputs-and-model-settings.sayOutLoud: Inputs are the blanks in a form letter, and settings are the dials. The temperature dial runs from steady to creative, and the safety dial sets how strict the filter is.

quiz.q: What does a lower temperature give you?
quiz.why: Lower temperatures lead to predictable results, and higher ones allow more varied responses.

quiz.q: Which is not allowed inside an input?
quiz.why: Learn says inputs cannot contain instructions, for security reasons.

quiz.q: Which model category suits data analysis and reasoning tasks?
quiz.why: Learn lists data analysis and reasoning as the use case for Deep models.

quiz.q: What is the default content moderation level?
quiz.why: Learn says the default moderation level for prompts is Moderate.

learn.title: Add inputs to your prompt
Change the model version and settings

ppai-code-interpreter-prompts.definition: With code interpreter, a prompt writes and runs Python to study data and return files, such as Excel sheets.

blocks.label: Python
blocks.plain: The prompt writes and runs code for analysis and charts.

blocks.label: File input
blocks.plain: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF files can be analyzed.

blocks.label: File output
blocks.plain: A prompt can return files, including Excel workbooks.

blocks.label: Billing
blocks.plain: Code generation and running count as premium generative AI features.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: An agent that uses it must use user authentication.

flow.label: Enable
flow.plain: A maker enables code interpreter in the prompt settings.

flow.label: Instruct
flow.plain: The maker writes clear instructions and names the output type.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The prompt writes and runs Python on the input data.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The prompt returns a result, such as an Excel file.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: The maker checks the output against the source.

example.input: A Contoso analyst gives a prompt a sales workbook and asks for a summary workbook.
example.output: The prompt runs Python on the data and returns a new Excel file with the totals.

whenToUse: You need data analysis, not only text answers.
You need an Excel or PDF file as the output.
Math or charts must be calculated, not guessed.
whenNot: One file in and one file out; no follow-up questions about that file.
Sovereign clouds are not supported yet.
It costs more: code generation counts as a premium feature.
ppai-code-interpreter-prompts.needToKnow: Code interpreter turns a prompt from a text writer into a data worker. It adds file output and Excel input and output, and it is billed as a premium generative AI feature. An agent that uses it must be set to use user authentication.
ppai-code-interpreter-prompts.demo: Give a prompt a small spreadsheet, ask for totals in a new Excel file, and download the result.
ppai-code-interpreter-prompts.askTheRoom: Which spreadsheet chore would you like a prompt to do for you?
ppai-code-interpreter-prompts.sayOutLoud: Without code interpreter, a prompt can only write words. With it, the prompt can also do the math and hand back a file. Tell it exactly what output you want.

quiz.q: What does code interpreter run?
quiz.why: Learn says agents that use it can write and run Python code.

quiz.q: Which of these is not supported?
options: Analyzing several files in one prompt
quiz.why: Learn lists analyzing multiple files in a single prompt as a limitation.

quiz.q: What must an agent use when it relies on code interpreter?
quiz.why: Learn says the agent must be configured to use user authentication.

quiz.q: How is code interpreter billed?
options: As a premium generative AI feature
quiz.why: Learn says code generation and execution count as premium text and generative AI features.

learn.title: Use code interpreter in a prompt to generate and execute Python code
Add inputs to your prompt

spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.definition: An agent in SharePoint answers questions from your content. New ones are made with Agent Builder, not as .agent files.

blocks.label: Agent Builder
blocks.plain: The tool used to create agents for SharePoint and OneDrive.

blocks.label: Knowledge
blocks.plain: You still pick SharePoint and OneDrive content as the agent's sources.

blocks.label: No agent file
blocks.plain: Creating an agent no longer saves an .agent file.

blocks.label: Old files
blocks.plain: Existing .agent files work until the end of March 2027.

blocks.label: Management
blocks.plain: You edit, share, and monitor agents in the Copilot app.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: A maker starts a new agent in Agent Builder.

flow.label: Ground
flow.plain: The maker picks SharePoint and OneDrive content as knowledge.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with questions the content can answer.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: The maker shares and monitors it through the Copilot app.

flow.label: Govern
flow.plain: Admins manage it through Agent 365.

example.input: A Contoso HR site owner wants a named policy helper for the site's content.
example.output: They build it in Agent Builder with the policy site as knowledge, and share it through the Copilot app.

whenToUse: You want a named question and answer, retrieval, or analysis agent.
People need the agent beyond one SharePoint site.
whenNot: For questions about only the current site, use Copilot in SharePoint directly.
For a repeatable task on a site, convert the agent to a skill.
Copilot Studio agents in SharePoint need no rebuild; publish them to the Copilot app.
spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.dataNote: Agent Builder follows the permissions and labels already set on your SharePoint and OneDrive files.
spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.needToKnow: Only the .agent file format is retiring, not agents in SharePoint and OneDrive. From mid-November 2026, new agents are built in Agent Builder and no longer save an .agent file. Existing .agent files work until the end of March 2027, then stop responding.
spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.demo: Show an agent built with one SharePoint site as knowledge, and ask it a question that only the site can answer.
spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.askTheRoom: Do you have any old .agent files that need an upgrade plan?
spai-build-agent-sharepoint-content.sayOutLoud: Think of it as a new door into the same room. Agents in SharePoint are not going away. Only the old file format is, so new agents are built in Agent Builder.

quiz.q: What is being retired?
quiz.why: Learn says only the .agent file format is being retired.

quiz.q: Where are new agents for SharePoint and OneDrive built?
quiz.why: From mid-November 2026, Agent Builder is used to create these agents.

quiz.q: When do existing .agent files stop responding?
quiz.why: Learn says existing .agent files work until the end of March 2027.

quiz.q: Which path suits questions about only the current site?
quiz.why: Learn recommends using Copilot in SharePoint directly for current-site questions.

learn.title: Upgrade agents in SharePoint and OneDrive
Build agents in Agent Builder

spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.definition: SharePoint knowledge sources are the files, folders, sites, or list that an Agent Builder agent searches to answer questions.

blocks.label: Files
blocks.plain: Up to 100 SharePoint files for each agent.

blocks.label: List
blocks.plain: One list per agent, up to 20,000 items or 50 megabytes.

blocks.label: Sites
blocks.plain: A site does not include its lists; add the list itself.

blocks.label: Permissions
blocks.plain: The agent respects existing permissions and sensitivity labels.

blocks.label: Readiness
blocks.plain: New files show a preparing status for several minutes.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: A maker picks the files, folders, sites, or list that hold the answers.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds them by link, search, or browsing.

flow.label: Wait
flow.plain: New files show a preparing status until they are ready.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: The maker asks a question only the content can answer.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The maker confirms the answer uses the expected source.

example.input: A Contoso HR agent should answer from the policy site and a leave-requests list.
example.output: The maker adds the site and the list separately, because a site does not include its lists.

whenToUse: The agent must answer from SharePoint content.
You can stay within the file and list limits.
You want to point the agent at specific files, folders, or sites.
whenNot: If Restricted SharePoint Search is on, SharePoint cannot be a source.
A list's attachments are not used to ground answers.
Agents answer Excel questions best when the data is on one sheet.
spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.dataNote: The agent follows the permissions and labels already set on SharePoint and OneDrive files.
spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.needToKnow: An agent can use up to 100 SharePoint files and one list. A list is cut off beyond 20,000 items or 50 megabytes, and its attachments are not used. Keep file contents short, and test with a question only the content can answer.
spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.demo: Add one site and one list, wait until both are ready, and ask a question that needs each one.
spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.askTheRoom: Which SharePoint library or list would your agent need to see first?
spai-agent-sharepoint-knowledge-sources.sayOutLoud: The agent can answer only from what you hand it. Point it at the files, folders, or lists that hold the answers, and it respects the permissions that already exist.

quiz.q: How many SharePoint files can one agent use?
quiz.why: Learn lists up to 100 SharePoint files for each agent.

quiz.q: If you add a SharePoint site, do its lists come along?
quiz.why: Selecting a site does not include its lists. To use a list, add that specific list.

quiz.q: Which part of a list is not used to ground answers?
quiz.why: The attachments column is not indexed or used for grounding.

quiz.q: What can block SharePoint as a knowledge source?
quiz.why: If Restricted SharePoint Search is enabled, you cannot use SharePoint as a knowledge source.

learn.title: Add knowledge sources to an agent in Agent Builder

cc-create-agent.definition: A Customer Conversation agent starts with a primary agent. It greets customers, finds their intent, and routes them to specialist sub-agents.

blocks.label: Primary agent
blocks.plain: Greets customers, finds the intent, and routes each conversation.

blocks.label: Sub-agents
blocks.plain: Specialists that each handle one focused task, such as billing.

blocks.label: Speech and chat
blocks.plain: Every agent supports both by default, so you pick no channel first.

blocks.label: Starting point
blocks.plain: Describe the scenario to get a draft, or start from a blank agent.

blocks.label: Contact center link
blocks.plain: Deploying to a contact center is done in a separate portal by an admin.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: A maker describes the customer scenario, in one or several messages.

flow.label: Generate
flow.plain: Copilot Studio drafts a primary agent with a name, description, and instructions.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: The maker reviews and adjusts the draft.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: The maker adds skills, tools, knowledge, and specialist sub-agents.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests the whole orchestration.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The maker publishes the agent and watches how it performs.

example.input: A Contoso help desk wants one front-door agent for billing and technical questions.
example.output: The primary agent sends billing questions to a billing agent and tech questions to a support agent.

whenToUse: Customer-facing scenarios such as contact centers and help desks.
You want specialist agents behind one front door.
You want one agent for both voice and chat.
whenNot: Building, testing, and evaluating can use Copilot Credits.
Deploying to a contact center needs a separate portal and an admin.

learn.title: Create an agent (Customer Conversation)

cc-instructions.definition: The description tells the orchestrator when to route to an agent. Instructions shape its tone and scope.

blocks.label: Description
blocks.plain: Up to 1,024 characters; tells the orchestrator when to route here.

blocks.label: General instructions
blocks.plain: Up to 20,000 characters that shape behavior, tone, and scope.

blocks.label: Speech and chat
blocks.plain: Only the primary agent gets separate guidance for calls and chat.

blocks.label: References
blocks.plain: Instructions can name tools, topics, variables, and sub-agents.

blocks.label: Context room
blocks.plain: Long instructions leave less room for the conversation.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: A maker writes what the agent handles, so routing works.

flow.label: General
flow.plain: The maker writes shared instructions: role, tone, and rules.

flow.label: Modes
flow.plain: The maker adds extra guidance for speech calls and for chat.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests behavior and routing.

flow.label: Trim
flow.plain: The maker shortens instructions to save conversation room.

example.input: A Contoso voice agent sounds too wordy on phone calls.
example.output: The maker adds speech guidance for short, warm replies, and keeps the chat guidance separate.

whenToUse: Your agent handles both phone calls and web chat.
Sub-agents need clearly different roles.
whenNot: Long instructions fill the context window and crowd out the conversation.
The agent can use only tools, topics, and sub-agents you added to it.
Do not repeat the same text in both the speech and chat guidance.

learn.title: Configure agent details and instructions (Customer Conversation)

cc-knowledge.definition: Knowledge sources ground a Customer Conversation agent's answers in your data, but sources that need sign-in work only in chat.

blocks.label: Direct sources
blocks.plain: Public websites, uploaded files, and Dynamics 365 can be added directly.

blocks.label: Sign-in sources
blocks.plain: SharePoint, Dataverse, Salesforce, and ServiceNow need sign-in settings first.

blocks.label: Chat only
blocks.plain: Sources that use end-user sign-in work in chat, not in speech.

blocks.label: Speech limit
blocks.plain: Speech channels do not support end-user sign-in.

blocks.label: Search quality
blocks.plain: For third-party sources, it depends on the provider's search.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: A maker picks the sources the agent needs.

flow.label: Authenticate
flow.plain: For sign-in sources, the maker sets authentication first.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds the source to the primary agent or a sub-agent.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests answers in chat.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: The maker decides what phone callers get without those sources.

example.input: A Contoso agent handles calls and chat, with a SharePoint source and a public help site.
example.output: Chat can use both sources. Phone calls can use only the public site, because callers cannot sign in.

whenToUse: You want answers grounded in your own data.
Some content is public and must work in both chat and speech.
whenNot: Do not depend on sign-in sources for phone conversations.
Third-party search quality depends on the provider's own search.
cc-knowledge.dataNote: Sources that use sign-in return only content the signed-in person can already access.

learn.title: Add knowledge to an agent (Customer Conversation)

cc-add-tools.definition: Tools let a Customer Conversation agent take actions and fetch live data, and the agent picks a tool by its name and description.

blocks.label: Tool types
blocks.plain: Prebuilt tools, prompts, Model Context Protocol servers, connectors, web services, and workflows.

blocks.label: Name and description
blocks.plain: Clear, specific text tells the agent when to use each tool.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: Some tools need you to sign in or give credentials first.

blocks.label: Actions
blocks.plain: For a connector with many actions, you pick which ones to offer.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: A maker picks a tool type that fits the system.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds the tool to the primary agent or a sub-agent.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker signs in or supplies credentials if needed.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: For a connector, the maker picks which actions to offer.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: The maker checks that the name and description are clear.

example.input: A Contoso agent must create support tickets.
example.output: The maker adds a tool named "Create support ticket" and describes when to use it and what it returns.

whenToUse: The agent must take actions or fetch live data.
A system already offers a connector, flow, or server.
whenNot: Avoid similar names across tools, skills, topics, and sub-agents.
Vague or overlapping descriptions make the agent pick the wrong tool.

learn.title: Add a tool to an agent (Customer Conversation)

mc-created-files.definition: In the Microsoft Copilot harness, an agent creates a file when a request needs one and returns it as a card you can download.

blocks.label: No setup
blocks.plain: You do not turn this on; the agent makes a file when the request needs one.

blocks.label: Built-in packages
blocks.plain: Python packages for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, tables, and charts.

blocks.label: File card
blocks.plain: The reply shows the file name, type, a preview, and a download link.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Up to 10 megabytes per file, kept 28 days after the last activity.

blocks.label: Follow-ups
blocks.plain: People can ask for changes to a created file in later turns.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for a report, sheet, deck, or chart.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: The agent writes the file with its built-in packages.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: The reply includes a file card below the message.

flow.label: Download
flow.plain: The person previews or downloads the file.

flow.label: Refine
flow.plain: The person asks for changes in a later turn.

example.input: A Contoso analyst asks for a sales summary and a chart of revenue by region.
example.output: The agent returns a file card for each, and the analyst asks for a taller chart in the next turn.

whenToUse: You need Word, Excel, PowerPoint, or PDF output.
People should refine a file over several turns.
whenNot: A file over 10 megabytes is not shown; ask the agent to split the output.
This feature is in preview and may change.
mc-created-files.dataNote: Created files are stored with the conversation and deleted 28 days after its last activity.

learn.title: Files the agent creates (Microsoft Copilot)

mc-triggers.definition: A trigger runs an autonomous agent when an event happens, such as an email arriving or a SharePoint item being created.

blocks.label: Trigger
blocks.plain: Sends event details to the agent when something happens.

blocks.label: Instructions and tools
blocks.plain: They decide what the agent does with the event details.

blocks.label: Run history
blocks.plain: Each run can start a new chat or continue the same session.

blocks.label: Credentials
blocks.plain: Run it as yourself, or share it so others use their own credentials.

blocks.label: Billing
blocks.plain: Autonomous use is billed at Copilot Studio rates for this harness.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: A maker adds the tools and writes instructions for the event.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds a trigger and sets its connection and options.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker starts a test event and adjusts the agent.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: The maker publishes; the agent does not run on its own before this.

flow.label: Activate
flow.plain: The maker runs it for themself, or shares it for others.

example.input: A Contoso team wants an agent to handle each new email on its own.
example.output: The trigger sends each email to the agent, which follows its instructions and uses its tools, one run at a time.

whenToUse: The agent should react to email, files, or schedules.
Work should start without a person chatting.
whenNot: The agent does not run on its own until it is published.
Republish after you change a trigger, instructions, or tools.
This feature is in preview and may change.
mc-triggers.dataNote: People you share it with use their own credentials, and their usage is billed through the environment that hosts the agent.

learn.title: Add triggers to an agent (Microsoft Copilot)

mc-foundry-iq.definition: Foundry IQ (a knowledge base built in Foundry) bundles data sources and search settings. Your agent connects to it as a tool.

blocks.label: Knowledge base
blocks.plain: Data sources plus search and ranking settings, built by another team.

blocks.label: Tool connection
blocks.plain: The agent uses it as a tool; only one is allowed per agent.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: Only knowledge bases you can reach in Foundry show up.

blocks.label: Sign-in types
blocks.plain: Key, certificate, service principal, or Microsoft Entra ID sign-in.

blocks.label: Tuning
blocks.plain: You tune the knowledge base in Foundry, not in Copilot Studio.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: Another team builds and tunes a knowledge base in Foundry.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker creates a connection and picks the knowledge base.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: The maker writes a detailed name and description to guide routing.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker asks a question and checks the activity trace.

flow.label: Tune
flow.plain: The knowledge base owner fixes poor results in Foundry.

example.input: A Contoso team already tuned a product knowledge base in Foundry.
example.output: The maker connects it to the agent as a tool, so the agent reuses that search setup instead of rebuilding it.

whenToUse: A team already built and tuned a knowledge base.
You want to reuse its search settings.
whenNot: An agent can have only one Foundry IQ connection.
Tune retrieval in Foundry, not in Copilot Studio.
It needs an agent built on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
mc-foundry-iq.dataNote: Removing the connection does not delete or change the knowledge base in Foundry.

learn.title: Connect to Foundry IQ from an agent (Microsoft Copilot)

knowledge-dataverse.definition: Dataverse knowledge grounds an agent in structured tables, so it can answer questions about business records.

blocks.label: Tables
blocks.plain: Up to 15 Dataverse tables per knowledge source.

blocks.label: Dataverse search
blocks.plain: An admin may need to turn it on before tables can be added.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: The agent must use Microsoft sign-in, and people see only data they can access.

blocks.label: Synonyms
blocks.plain: Short names for columns help the model read cryptic table names.

blocks.label: Glossary
blocks.plain: Definitions for business terms and acronyms, such as overdue task.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: A maker picks the Dataverse tables the agent needs.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: The maker writes a detailed name and description.

flow.label: Synonyms
flow.plain: The maker adds synonyms for cryptic column names.

flow.label: Glossary
flow.plain: The maker adds definitions for business terms.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with questions about specific records.

example.input: A person asks for VP (vice president) contacts, but the table stores the value Vice President.
example.output: A glossary entry says VP means Vice President, so the agent finds the right records.

whenToUse: You need answers about specific business records.
Your data already lives in Dataverse tables.
whenNot: Dataverse tables need Microsoft sign-in; the other sign-in choices are not supported.
Missing permissions can hide tables during setup.
Glossary changes can take up to 15 minutes to apply.
knowledge-dataverse.dataNote: People see only the data they have permission to access.

learn.title: Add Dataverse tables as a knowledge source

knowledge-tuning.definition: Knowledge settings control whether an agent may answer without a source, whether it searches the web, and how it cites sources.

blocks.label: Ungrounded answers
blocks.plain: A setting that allows or blocks answers made without a source or tool.

blocks.label: Citations
blocks.plain: With that setting off, an answer needs a citation or it is withheld.

blocks.label: Web search
blocks.plain: Adds broad results from Bing, which you can turn off.

blocks.label: Citation instructions
blocks.plain: Telling the model to cite sources makes answers more consistent.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: A maker decides if general-knowledge answers are acceptable.

flow.label: Block
flow.plain: If not, the maker blocks answers made without a source or tool.

flow.label: Web
flow.plain: The maker turns web search on or off to match approved sources.

flow.label: Cite
flow.plain: The maker adds instructions to cite sources every time.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker repeats questions and checks answers and citations.

example.input: A Contoso agent answers a follow-up about sale items from chat history, with no source.
example.output: With ungrounded answers off, that reply is blocked and the fallback topic runs.

whenToUse: Only approved sources should answer.
You want a clear failure when no source or tool is used.
whenNot: Turning it off does not guarantee the model uses no general knowledge.
A correct answer without a citation can be withheld, and it may come and go.
These settings need generative orchestration turned on.

learn.title: Knowledge sources summary

flow-prompt-nodes.definition: A prompt node makes one AI call inside an agent flow and returns text, JSON, or a Word document to the next steps.

blocks.label: One call
blocks.plain: A single AI call, with no tool orchestration or data browsing.

blocks.label: Instructions
blocks.plain: Content from earlier steps must be placed in its instructions.

blocks.label: Output type
blocks.plain: Text, JSON, or a document, based on what later steps need.

blocks.label: Limits
blocks.plain: Dataverse is the only knowledge source; code interpreter is the only tool.

blocks.label: Harness note
blocks.plain: Microsoft Copilot harness workflows use an agent action instead.

flow.label: Gather
flow.plain: Earlier flow steps collect the data.

flow.label: Insert
flow.plain: That data is placed into the prompt node's instructions.

flow.label: Run
flow.plain: The prompt node makes one AI call.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: It returns text, JSON, or a document.

flow.label: Continue
flow.plain: Later steps use the named fields or the text.

example.input: A Contoso flow gets a customer email and needs its topic, sentiment, and urgency.
example.output: A prompt node returns JSON with those three fields, and the next step reads each one by name.

whenToUse: You need one focused AI step inside a fixed flow.
Later steps need named fields, not free text.
whenNot: It sees only what is in its instructions.
It cannot orchestrate tools or browse data.
It is not available in Microsoft Copilot harness workflows.

learn.title: Add a prompt node to an agent flow

servicenow-integration.definition: The ServiceNow connector lets a Copilot Studio agent create, read, and update records, such as incidents, in your service desk.

blocks.label: Premium connector
blocks.plain: A premium connector with create, read, and update actions.

blocks.label: Any table
blocks.plain: Its actions work on any ServiceNow table, so access must be limited.

blocks.label: Integration account
blocks.plain: Use a dedicated account with only the roles it needs.

blocks.label: Instance address
blocks.plain: Only instance addresses ending in service-now.com are supported.

blocks.label: Knowledge option
blocks.plain: ServiceNow can also be a real-time knowledge source, in preview.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: A team decides which tables and actions the agent may use.

flow.label: Account
flow.plain: An admin creates a least-privilege integration account.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker adds the connector and signs in with that account.

flow.label: Pick
flow.plain: The maker offers only the actions the agent needs.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with a known incident.

example.input: A Contoso service desk wants an agent that looks up an incident by its number.
example.output: The agent calls a read action through a least-privilege account, and write actions stay off until they are needed.

whenToUse: A service desk agent must act on live incident data.
People should look up or create records by chat.
whenNot: Instructions reduce risk but are not a security control.
Deny write access to approvals, roles, and credentials.
Other web addresses can cause connection errors.
servicenow-integration.dataNote: The connector can reach any table, so give the account only the roles and table rules it needs.

learn.title: ServiceNow

snowflake-integration.definition: The Snowflake connector lets an agent run database queries on a Snowflake warehouse and use the results.

blocks.label: Premium connector
blocks.plain: A premium connector; use the current version 2, not the older one.

blocks.label: Custom queries
blocks.plain: It runs the Structured Query Language (SQL) statement you give it.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: It supports Microsoft Entra ID external OAuth sign-in.

blocks.label: Network
blocks.plain: It works with Azure Private Link and virtual networks.

blocks.label: Clouds
blocks.plain: It is not offered in US Government clouds.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: A team decides which data and queries the agent may run.

flow.label: Sign-in
flow.plain: An admin sets up Microsoft Entra external OAuth with Snowflake.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds the version 2 connector to the agent.

flow.label: Query
flow.plain: The agent runs a scoped statement and gets the results.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The maker checks the results against the warehouse.

example.input: A Contoso analyst asks an agent for last quarter's totals by region.
example.output: The agent runs a scoped statement through the connector and summarizes the rows it gets back.

whenToUse: The agent must run specific queries on warehouse data.
You want governed sign-in to the warehouse.
whenNot: The older Snowflake connector is deprecated; use version 2.
It is not offered in US Government clouds.

learn.title: Snowflake

sap-integration.definition: SAP (business software) has two connectors. One calls functions through a gateway, and one works with OData data.

blocks.label: Business functions
blocks.plain: The enterprise resource planning (ERP) connector calls SAP functions through a gateway.

blocks.label: SAP OData connector
blocks.plain: Creates, reads, updates, and deletes OData entities.

blocks.label: Not full OData
blocks.plain: It is not a full implementation of the OData protocol.

blocks.label: Premium
blocks.plain: Both are premium connectors in Copilot Studio.

blocks.label: Virtual networks
blocks.plain: With a virtual network, the OData connector cannot use the gateway.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: A team picks the ERP connector or the OData connector.

flow.label: Prepare
flow.plain: An admin sets up the gateway and SAP permissions.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds the connector and signs in.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: The maker offers narrow, read-first operations.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with a known record.

example.input: A Contoso finance agent must check an invoice's status.
example.output: The agent calls one narrow read operation and returns the status, with no write actions added yet.

whenToUse: Your SAP system exposes OData services.
You need to call SAP business functions.
whenNot: Plan the gateway and SAP permissions before you build.
The OData connector is not the full OData protocol.
sap-integration.dataNote: The ERP connector reaches SAP through an on-premises data gateway.

learn.title: SAP ERP
SAP OData

salesforce-integration.definition: Salesforce can feed an agent two ways: a premium connector for actions, or a real-time knowledge source, which is in preview.

blocks.label: Premium connector
blocks.plain: Gives the agent actions that work on Salesforce records.

blocks.label: Real-time knowledge
blocks.plain: A preview source that searches Salesforce at run time.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: The Salesforce account needs API (programmatic) access.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: Signing in with a Salesforce custom domain is not supported.

blocks.label: Cloud fit
blocks.plain: The connector is not offered in some Government clouds.

flow.label: Choose
flow.plain: A team picks the connector or the knowledge source.

flow.label: Check
flow.plain: An admin confirms API access and the cloud fit.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker adds it and signs in with a supported method.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: The maker picks only the tables or records needed.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests with a known case.

example.input: A Contoso city services agent must tell residents the status of their case.
example.output: The agent reads one case record through Salesforce, using only the fields it needs.

whenToUse: Answers need current customer relationship management (CRM) records.
You want case status without copying data.
whenNot: Trial accounts have no API access, so they cannot be used.
Create and update actions do not support nested objects or multi-select picklists.
salesforce-integration.dataNote: The knowledge source runs at request time using the signed-in person's own access.

learn.title: Salesforce
Add Power Platform connectors as knowledge (preview)

jira-integration.definition: The Jira connector lets an agent find and update issues, so people get status in the chat.

blocks.label: Premium connector
blocks.plain: A premium connector with direct issue and project actions.

blocks.label: Token sign-in
blocks.plain: A token is used for access; password sign-in is deprecated.

blocks.label: Search lag
blocks.plain: Recent changes may not show in search results right away.

blocks.label: Return limits
blocks.plain: At most 20 comments and 40 changelog items come back.

blocks.label: Firewall
blocks.plain: A Jira server behind a firewall is not supported.

flow.label: Plan
flow.plain: A team decides which projects and actions the agent may use.

flow.label: Token
flow.plain: A maker creates a token in Jira for the connection.

flow.label: Add
flow.plain: The maker adds the connector and picks the actions.

flow.label: Look up
flow.plain: The agent fetches an issue by its key.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The maker checks the result against Jira.

example.input: A Contoso support agent is asked what is blocking a release issue.
example.output: The agent looks up the issue by its key and summarizes the blocker and the next step.

whenToUse: People need issue status inside the conversation.
Your Jira site is reachable from the cloud.
whenNot: Search results can lag behind recent writes, so look up by issue key to test.
Basic sign-in with a password is deprecated.

learn.title: Jira

epic-fhir-integration.definition: The FHIRlink connector lets an agent use records on FHIR (a health data standard) services, including Epic.

blocks.label: Premium connector
blocks.plain: A premium connector with create, read, update, and delete actions.

blocks.label: Providers
blocks.plain: It works with Azure Health Data Services, Google, and Epic on FHIR.

blocks.label: Epic sign-in
blocks.plain: You bring your own Epic app, with its address, client ID, and secret.

blocks.label: Direct access
blocks.plain: It reads the FHIR service directly, without copying data into Dataverse.

blocks.label: Call limit
blocks.plain: 100 calls per connection every 60 seconds.

flow.label: Register
flow.plain: An admin sets up the Epic app registration and approvals.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker adds the connector with the Epic details.

flow.label: Scope
flow.plain: The maker offers only the read actions the scenario needs.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks for a specific patient lookup.

flow.label: Verify
flow.plain: The maker checks results against the source system.

example.input: A Contoso clinic agent needs to look up one patient's record in Epic.
example.output: The agent calls one read action through the connector and returns only the fields the task needs.

whenToUse: You need live access to a FHIR service.
You do not want to copy clinical data into another store.
whenNot: Setup needs administrative access for the app registrations.
Check your own privacy and compliance rules before you connect clinical data.
epic-fhir-integration.dataNote: Sharing with other people requires each person to create their own connection.

learn.title: FHIRlink

shopify-integration.definition: For Shopify, use a preview connector for orders, or build your own custom connector.

blocks.label: Ready-made option
blocks.plain: A preview connector for orders, built by an Independent Publisher.

blocks.label: Custom connector
blocks.plain: You import a file that describes the operations.

blocks.label: Your choice
blocks.plain: A custom connector exposes only the operations you pick.

blocks.label: Sign-in
blocks.plain: The ready-made connector uses an access token.

blocks.label: Size limit
blocks.plain: The OpenAPI 2.0 file must be under 1 megabyte.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: A team picks the ready-made or custom connector.

flow.label: Describe
flow.plain: For a custom connector, the maker imports the OpenAPI file.

flow.label: Trim
flow.plain: The maker keeps only the approved operations.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: The maker signs in with an access token.

flow.label: Test
flow.plain: The maker tests an order lookup.

example.input: A Contoso retail agent should answer order questions but must not change orders.
example.output: The maker exposes only an order lookup and leaves out refunds and cancellations.

whenToUse: A support agent needs order facts from Shopify.
You want to control which operations the agent can call.
whenNot: OpenAPI 3.0 files are not supported; the file must be 2.0.
The ready-made connector is a preview and may change.

learn.title: Create a custom connector from an OpenAPI definition
Shopify (Independent Publisher) (Preview)
